public_statements.boeing:
When I came in, I said our priority, far and away, was debt, and that we'd do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing were ready. We've done the first part. The balance sheet is repaired, the 777X is delivering, the 737 MAX family is certified, and the 737 line is building steadily at 57 a month. A lot of people did hard work the right way to get here. I think we've turned the ship. Now the job is to keep it steady.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. The work on our next single-aisle goes on, in stages and with the data in front of us. We've asked all three engine makers to bring us their best proposals, with durability proven before entry into service. When we do launch, it will be on a conservative plan with headroom in it, and we will not take on fixed-price development risk.

On production, we'll keep the 737 where it is and keep it stable. A rate step only comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity. We'll keep adding 787 capacity in Charleston as our customers need it. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class. The financials will follow our production performance.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early. We'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft, for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. This is the Airbus of the 2030s that we have been preparing for: a step change in efficiency, built on technologies we have matured and demonstrated, the wing first among them, and on a production system designed together with the aircraft. We will invite CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to power it, so that our customers have a choice of engine and our ramp-up has secure supply. The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle offer. We will keep its lines running alongside the new aircraft's ramp-up, giving our customers a long and orderly transition. On widebodies our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. We will continue a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, and we are securing key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. The programme is funded from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run 2030, and every year after.

Here's what we know. Our airframer customers are working on their next narrowbody plans. What they launch, and when, is their call, not ours. Whatever they launch, CFM will offer an engine for it, and we're working closely with both of them, privately, on what that aircraft needs. We don't have a birthright on that next order, and we won't act like we do.

RISE stays fully funded as our technology programme with our partners at Safran, and testing goes on. We won't put an entry-into-service date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it, and on what we know today that is 2045 at the earliest. Meanwhile, what we learn there keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet.

On the widebody, we're investing in the GEnx for our 787 customers.

Here's what we don't know: which aircraft launch, when, and with what engines. When we know, you'll know. Until then we keep getting after LEAP durability and deliveries with our supply base. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney: Bad news first. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has slipped from 26.7% in 2026 to 24.4% in 2029 as the market mix moved, though we still deliver our full share of the A320neo. We control what we can control. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it, as sole or shared source, provided GTF2 can be ready by that airframe's entry into service. GTF2 is ready six years from launch, so a launch this year is ready in 2036. It will not enter service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. It builds on the durability work we are doing on the GTF fleet today. The offer is on standard terms, with no launch discounts; these are responsible bets with responsible paybacks. We are not committing to a Joint Venture today. We will consider one only once a partner's commitment, or an airframer's demand for one, is on the record, and any partnership will share risk and investment, never our core technology. The airframers will speak for their own programmes. The dividend comes first, and this plan needs no change to it or to our path on debt.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for a new single-aisle in the round an airframer selects it. Not before. UltraFan is more efficient than any other engine available, and we have done the work without waiting. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch, with support and MRO in place, through partner shops, before entry into service. Our preference is partnership. The Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit when our partner does. No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle
boeing.detail: We invite all three narrowbody engine makers (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce) to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. Selection will be on value among engines actually launched, with proven durability before entry into service as a contract condition. No fps date and no launch commitment. This serves the dual- or triple-source engine enabler (unmet today). The engine code is decided at launch: code 3 (CFM) by default, or code 7 if P&W and Rolls-Royce can be ready by EIS.

boeing.move: Hold the 737 at 57 a month with KPI gates and stability first
boeing.detail: No rate step requested. KPIs are monitored monthly. Confirm the LEAP-1B allocation with CFM at today's rate, and keep the FAA-agreed process in place for any future step.

boeing.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
boeing.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

airbus.move: Secure our own supply for the NGSA ramp
airbus.detail: Keep the NGSA wing in-house: Wing of Tomorrow and the run-at-rate demonstrator, with aerostructures through Airbus Atlantic, Airbus Aerostructures and the ex-Spirit sites. Secure titanium and forgings through the Aubert & Duval co-ownership and additive (DED) parts. Extend the critical raw-materials and rare-earths watchlist to NGSA. This covers our own ramp only and makes no claim on any rival's capacity [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

airbus.move: Multi-source engine strategy and long-term capacity agreements
airbus.detail: Open NGSA propulsion to CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce (code 7). Seek long-term capacity agreements with CFM covering the A320neo and NGSA from 2035. Certify CFM first and further makers as their engines mature, as on the A320neo. The aim is supply certainty, not leverage [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

airbus.move: Orderly A320neo family transition (Alt supply plan)
airbus.detail: Keep the A320neo lines running longer alongside the NGSA ramp. The steps are a ceiling, never above today's rate, and NGSA has first claim on resources. The plan is re-checked at the 2035 gate and reverts to base on a supply crunch, an engine slip or a quality event. The cost is budgeted from NGSA entry into service.
Work with the European and US industry associations, Boeing included, to keep civil aerospace on a tariff-free, zero-for-zero footing [AX-0088, AX-0046].

airbus.move: Skills for the Airbus of the 2030s
airbus.detail: Run apprenticeship, graduate and university programmes in Europe to grow NGSA engineering and production talent from our own pipeline. This is recruitment for the Airbus of the 2030s and targets no rival [AX-0073, A-0330].

cfm.move: Offer a CFM engine for any new narrowbody either airframer launches, at minimum a LEAP derivative
cfm.detail: H1: we never refuse an airframer and never lock one out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. This is a product offer only, with no price, terms or concession [CX-0184]. It is what CFM does today on the 737 MAX and A320neo, so it fits joint practice and Safran's consent is assumed (inference). The board does not price it.

cfm.move: RISE stays funded as a technology programme with Safran: ground, durability and dust testing continue; no product launch and no entry-into-service date
cfm.detail: H5: no cancel, and no programme dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398]. RISE becomes a product when an airframer wants it [CX-0469, CX-0205]. RISE is a joint programme with Safran, and continuing it as technology is joint practice. Ali's floor applies: no Open Fan before 2045, and that is a floor, not a promise. RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades [CX-0162].

cfm.move: LEAP durability kits and supply-base work (FLIGHT DECK) continue ahead of any new programme
cfm.detail: Safety, quality, delivery, cost [CX-0658]. 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613]. We fix the supply base we have before we load it with a new programme (lean before capital) [CX-0540, CX-0653].

pratt_whitney.move: GTF fleet durability kit (Hot Section kit) offered through MRO at value
pratt_whitney.detail: We keep offering the GTF durability upgrade to operators through our MRO network at value. It is sold, not given away, and it is not tied to any airframe campaign [PX-0088][PX-0100]. It has no effect on the game board. It keeps the fleet ahead of a new engine [PX-0080].

pratt_whitney.move: Standard commercial terms on GTF2; no launch-style discounts
pratt_whitney.detail: Any GTF2 offer to Airbus or Boeing is on standard terms. There is no launch discount, concession or free upgrade to win a selection [PX-0055]. Mitchill's ground 3 (terms) passes. A rival's price does not move the answer.

rolls_royce.detail: No concessions to buy narrowbody or widebody share. Win-win terms, value remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

rolls_royce.move: Narrowbody support plan through partner shops
rolls_royce.detail: If an airframer selects UltraFan, the support plan goes live: a partner-shop network on the Singapore Joint Venture model, repair technology qualified in those shops, a spare-engine pool and an early-years intervention team, all in place before entry into service [RX-0283, RX-0287]. No dates are disclosed.

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture open to Pratt & Whitney
rolls_royce.detail: Rolls-Royce commits to the Joint Venture once Pratt & Whitney's commitment is on the public record, on terms that credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings [RX-0072, RX-0118]. No Joint Venture date is disclosed.

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan technology demonstration and Trent time-on-wing work continue
rolls_royce.detail: The self-funded UltraFan narrowbody technology work continues inside a flat R&D envelope [RX-0094, RX-0214]. The durability and time-on-wing programme on the installed Trent fleet continues [RX-0123]. No new programme is launched.

boeing.move: Staged fps business case for the 2035 round (authority-to-offer work)
boeing.detail: Solo by default. Compare the 7-year and 10-year ramps on the 2035 grid under the Board's rule: take the 10-year ramp only where it sits within $1B of the 7-year in every plausible column, otherwise the ramp with the higher worst column. Compare Renton with new sites, including a MAX bridge plan so the Renton wind-down follows the fps's actual ramp, not its plan. Carry Malave's risk-case column and the slip priors. Sequence the fps against any 787 Re-engine under H4. No date, no fixed-price development.

boeing.move: Keep 787 Re-engine readiness warm (study only, no launch)
boeing.detail: Covers engineering definition, an engine-durability requirement with the engine makers, new-part supplier readiness (rate breaks only when supplier output is there, as on the 787 heat exchangers [B-2308]) and a certification plan with the type certificate before building at rate, so no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. Re-test it on the 2035 grid only if the A350 has not been re-engined (H3, second half). No programme spend committed.

boeing.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
boeing.detail: Embedded staff, buffers and second sources where possible, so supplier readiness is never the reason a future programme slips.
Net debt is at the historical level. Allocating the surplus cash is the Board's decision, so nothing is said publicly.

airbus.detail: Hold a Board and ExCo gate in 2035 covering three questions. First, NGSA technology and production-system maturity and schedule margin, since a one-year slip lands in 2038. Second, whether the Alt plan should stand or revert to base. Third, the A350 Re-engine test with full overlap and peak cash: Toepfer's preview shows $6.67B a year in 2035-36, which fails the $5.2B line unless spend starts after 2036, and rule 3 applies if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine.

cfm.move: Private product and technology-roadmap talks with both airframers on their next narrowbody
cfm.detail: Talks on platforms stay private [CX-0586]. We want to be on all the critical platforms [CX-0587]. The goal is to learn requirements and timing first-hand, not to sell a date.

cfm.move: Ducted decision staged to the 2035 round
cfm.detail: No money committed and no date given. It gets re-tested on the 2035 grid if any of these lands on the record: an airframer selection that puts CFM next to a rival (an S2- or S5-type column); a rival new narrowbody engine launched, committed or selected (H3); or a 2035 grid showing the Ducted ahead of hold by more than $1B. Ali's conditions carry over: a cross-functional durability plan for the hot section, no ready year before launch + 6, and the Ducted is never called the next generation.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 durability programme staged for a triggered launch
pratt_whitney.detail: If launch_if_selected fires, testing starts at launch at Advantage level (3x the base programme) under severe-environment conditions [PX-0084][PX-0128]. GTF2 stays a derivative of the geared architecture. Every life-limited part is at full life at entry into service, and no endurance testing is traded for schedule. If test data put readiness past a selecting airframe's EIS, the EIS moves and the testing does not. Fleet spares keep priority over GTF2 test hardware (Eddy). The 2035 cancel test for a live 2030 GTF2 follows Mitchill's rule: cancel only if the 2035 brief's cancel row beats its hold row, judged on the remaining $0.33B.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce: no commitment; revisit in 2035
pratt_whitney.detail: We revisit only if Rolls-Royce commits on the public record or a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). If we commit, P&W keeps the gear and the core as its own modules, with no licence or transfer [P-1233].

rolls_royce.detail: Watson's gates, which apply only if the option triggers: partner-shop agreements signed in the trigger year, capacity qualified by 2036, support live by the first entry into service. Gearbox, casting and forging capacity pre-qualified with high-performing suppliers. No spend before the trigger. Testing never bends to an airframer's date; if maturity slips, we tell the airframer early.

If the option triggers and the airframer later drops Rolls-Royce from its code before entry into service, McCabe books the cancel arithmetic ($8B x 5/7 = $5.71B for a 2035 cancel), not the sunk cost, and the orphan programme is cancelled ('that activity is gone') [R-1573].

boeing.public_statement:
When I came in, I said our priority, far and away, was debt, and that we'd do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing were ready. We've done the first part. The balance sheet is repaired, the 777X is delivering, the 737 MAX family is certified, and the 737 line is building steadily at 57 a month. A lot of people did hard work the right way to get here. I think we've turned the ship. Now the job is to keep it steady.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. The work on our next single-aisle goes on, in stages and with the data in front of us. We've asked all three engine makers to bring us their best proposals, with durability proven before entry into service. When we do launch, it will be on a conservative plan with headroom in it, and we will not take on fixed-price development risk.

On production, we'll keep the 737 where it is and keep it stable. A rate step only comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity. We'll keep adding 787 capacity in Charleston as our customers need it. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class. The financials will follow our production performance.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early. We'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever. fps hold (new_site, engine code null), rate_737 hold, re787 hold. Every field is at its default, so no item goes to the Board. The package below answers what it asked to see.

H1 AND H3 RULINGS FOR 2030 (management's call, with evidence)
- H1 (no fps in Round 1) is lifted because its 2026 grounds have lapsed. The 777X delivers from 2027 [BX-0550] and is cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547]. The MAX 7/10 certified in 2026 [BX-1299, BX-1873]. Net debt is $0.0B at end-2029 in the brief (end-2030 in stress, $3.3B at end-2029) [BX-1305, B-2327]. In July 2026 I put us about two years from financial readiness [BG-0068]. The grid, not the rule, holds the fps back.
- H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): lifted on the same grounds. Its reason was the 777X first [B-2276].
- H3, second half, stays in force: no 787 Re-engine once the A350 Re-engine has launched. Nothing is on the record.
- Other rules: H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger. No certification trouble is reported, so the FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309]. H4, H5, H6 and H8 apply as written.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief reports no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The MAX delivered 510/594/624/654 to plan in 2026-29. Pope's KPI veto is not invoked.
2. Are market, technology and the balance sheet ready? The balance sheet is ready (net debt $0 in base and stress through 2050). Technology passes on the board. The market case is not ready: every fps row loses $2.08B to about $22B against Do Nothing in every column [BX-1296].
3. What if certification takes longer? Malave's buffer test (S6 against Do Nothing −0.02; the line is −2.02):
   - Fail (binding): every stand-alone fps row. The best, 10-year at Renton, is −3.47.
   - Pass: Do Nothing (0.00 gap), Re-engine (+3.28), Rate Increase (−0.71) and Rate Increase + Re-engine (+2.59).
4. Is this doing less, better? The Rate Increase sits within ε of Do Nothing in every column, so the smaller plan wins [BX-1239].

fps: HOLD
- Malave's veto binds on every 10-year, 7-year and via-Embraer row without the Re-engine. It also binds on 10-year + rate + Re-engine (−2.80; −2.22 at Renton, a narrow fail).
- Two fps rows pass his buffer: 10-year + Re-engine at Renton (−1.27) and at new sites (−1.78). Both sit 3.18 to 5.06 below the Re-engine alone in every column. Both are at H4's 2-year overlap limit with no slack, and the Board would veto both items.
- Via Embraer is about $18B worse than the Solo 10-year in every column, with a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty. Pope's IP test finds it adds nothing Boeing lacks.
- Objective premium for 50/50: $0. Chasing it costs at least $2.17B against the best plan in any column ($4.52B in S2), above the $2B cap.
- The future is built alongside the first three priorities [BX-1245]: a staged 2035 case (other move).

787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD (the hard call; I came in leaning to bring it)
- Item value: +3.30 in S1, S2, S3 and S6; −2.48 in S4 and S5.
- In my expected column, S2, it is the best plan by $3.30B, and it passes the buffer by $3.30B. Three things move me to hold.
- (a) The Board has said it will veto it under its −$1B per-item downside line, which counts every plausible column. The bulletin rules out no A350 Re-engine. Its veto binds and I have no override against it. Bringing an item I know will be vetoed is not proof before commitment [BG-0021].
- (b) Malave, my independent check [BX-1316], puts an A350 Re-engine this round at 40-50%.
  - The basis is company doctrine (profile §7): Airbus re-engines cheaply (the A330neo [B-2446]), expect an early attempt, and the widebody is a Chicken game.
  - Weighted, the edge is 3.30 − 5.78p = $0.41-0.99B, inside ε.
  - Inside ε, the higher worst column decides (Do Nothing −2.64 against −5.12 in S5), as do doing less [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548].
  - Doctrine, not my record, drove this probability read: I have no statement on Airbus's next airplane (Low), and Malave's seat is thin (Low).
- (c) My appetite for technology and launch risk is low; slow is fast [BX-1291].
- Cost logged separately as a Board-downside hold, not against the cap: $3.30B given up in S1, S2, S3 and S6; $2.48B saved in S4 and S5.
- Cost of waiting:
  - If the A350 moves first, H3 closes the Re-engine for good.
  - If not, a 2035 Re-engine (EIS 2040) overlaps a 2035 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B strain, at H4's limit) or a 7-year fps by 5 years (an H4 breach). The 2035 case must sequence them.
  - The 2035 grid will price this; I won't guess it.
- Pope's readiness results all pass (engineering free, Charleston, supplier gate, no concurrency). The programme is ready to bring once its market risk is acceptable.

737 RATE: HOLD
- Item value: −0.69 in S2 (expected); +0.09 only in S1 and S4; −0.69 to −0.71 in the NGSA columns.
- With any fps in the row it is −0.90 to −1.04 in every column. Its gain rests on nobody ever launching a new narrowbody, and our own plan carries a 2035 fps case.
- It lowers the worst column (S5 −3.34 against −2.64).
- The KPI gate is open. Pope says operations could deliver 57, then 62, then about 65 with slack, with the LEAP-1B allocation as a condition. FAA agreement would be sought step by step and has not been requested.
- This is a judgement on our own plan and production readiness, not on Airbus (H6).
- Doctrine's 'Rate Increase in Turn 1' (§6) rested on superseded engine numbers in which the rate added value alongside the fps. On this board that reverses (dashboard_game.md §5).
- The deferral is a loss we accept in S1 and S4 ($0.09B), not a wait.

ENGINE CODE AND SITE
- Engine code: null, since nothing is launched. At launch: code 3 by default, or code 7 if P&W and Rolls-Royce can be ready by EIS.
- Site: new_site. Renton changes nothing without a launch and is decided in 2035 with a MAX bridge plan.

BOARD PACKAGE
- Submitted row (Do Nothing): S1 +0.00 / S2 −0.02 / S3 −1.01 / S4 −2.62 / S5 −2.64 / S6 −0.02. No Board items, since each field is at its default.
- Expected column: S2. S6 is −0.02, 0.00 against Do Nothing. Buffer: pass. Fundable when the 777X turns: pass on timing.
- Net debt: $0 by end-2029 in base and end-2030 in stress, held to 2050.
- Premiums: soft $0 and objective $0. The Re-engine hold is logged separately, as above.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's binding veto struck every stand-alone fps row; none was ordered.
- Pope's KPI veto was not invoked.
- No overrides.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave's memo was the decisive input, weighed as my independent check [BX-1316]. His buffer veto binds; his other views are advice from a thin seat (one call, Low confidence).
- Buffer test: I accept it and his corrections. Two fps + Re-engine rows pass, not one. S6 is 4.55 below the Re-engine alone, not 4.52. 10-year Renton + rate + Re-engine fails narrowly at −2.22. No stand-alone fps row is ordered.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: I accept his pass on timing. The cash does not hold the fps back; the grid and the buffer do.
- Debt penalty: I accept that it is already netted and must not be subtracted again.
- Rate: I accept that its +0.09 cannot be shown to survive our own 2035 plan.
- What moved me was his 40-50% read of an A350 Re-engine this round. He drew it from company doctrine (§7), not his record. It puts the Re-engine's weighted edge ($0.41-0.99B) inside ε, where the higher worst column and doing less decide. Together with the Board's announced veto, that turned my lean to bring the Re-engine into a hold.
- I also log his offer: he would concur on the buffer if the Re-engine were brought, and he would change his mind on evidence the A350 stays put. That is the 2035 trigger.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope's seat runs on [NOW] operations doctrine with no airplane-business evidence (Very low confidence), so I weighed it as gates, not judgement.
- I accept her gate results: KPI gate open and her veto not invoked; zero strain with the fps on hold; a 2030 Re-engine clears any 2035 fps; via Embraer adds no IP or capacity; the Renton caveat that a MAX wind-down must follow the fps's actual ramp.
- Her rate path (57, then 62, then about 65, with up to a year of slack) and the LEAP-1B allocation condition go into the record. They show the hold rests on value, not readiness.
- Her Re-engine readiness results all pass. She recommended launching it if Kelly and the Board carry its market risk. The Board has said it will not carry that risk (−2.48 in S4/S5 breaks its −$1B line), and Malave's read puts the weighted edge inside ε. So I did not take her launch recommendation. Her readiness findings make it bringable in 2035 if the A350 has not moved.
- Her derivative slip prior (+2 years, unpriced) is noted for that case.

cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the buffer test as the baseline, not a sensitivity. The balance sheet is where we said it would be: net debt at zero by end-2029, 2030 in the stress case, and it holds on every Re-engine and Rate Increase row. So the question is which baseline we can meet and potentially beat.

fps: every stand-alone row fails my buffer. The best, the 10-year ramp at Renton, sits $3.45B below Do Nothing in S6. That veto binds. The 7-year and Embraer rows miss by $6B to $23B. It is fundable now the 777X has turned; the grid, not the cash, holds it back. Bring the staged case in 2035.

787 Re-engine: it clears my buffer by $3.30B, and a 2030 start spends its $5B before a 2035 fps does. I will not veto it. But its worst column is $2.48B below Do Nothing, and our doctrine expects an early A350 Re-engine. At a 40-50% chance its edge is $0.4-1.0B, inside ε, where I take the higher worst column. With the Board's -$1B line, my advice is hold, logging the $3.30B as a Board-downside cost.

Rate Increase: the gate is open on the record, subject to Stephanie's KPIs and the FAA. But its +$0.09B assumes nobody ever launches a new narrowbody, and our plan does. It is -$0.69B in S2 and lowers the worst column. Hold.

My guidance: Do Nothing, barring evidence the A350 stays put. A higher confidence plan, and we're bullish on 2035.

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness (doctrine; answers the CEO's ask 3)
tests.threshold: Engineering free, Charleston capacity, engine maker and durability, supplier gate, and a certification plan with no production-certification concurrency.
tests.numbers: Engineering: no major development in flight in 2030, so one development at a time holds. Charleston: the expansion doubles the footprint for 787 rates in the teens. The board's 787 is 100 a year (8.3 a month); a lone Re-engine gaining 1 pp a year from 58.8% reaches about 64% (108 a year, 9 a month) by 2040 and 85% (145 a year, 12 a month) at the cap, within the teens. Engine maker and durability: neither is priced on the board nor in the brief; make durability maturity a contract condition (other move). Certification: type certificate before building at rate, with no concurrency. EIS is 2035 nominal and 2037 central on the doctrine prior. Supplier gate as above.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand (inference, one remark)
tests.threshold: Back the Rate Increase where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column; otherwise not applicable.
tests.numbers: Demand is visible: the waiting backlog is 799 (2030), 1,149 (2032), 1,319 (2033), 1,174 (2034), 763 (2035), 419 (2036) and 0 from 2038. But the grid prices the extra capacity at -0.69 in the CEO's expected column S2 (-0.69 to -0.71 in S2, S3, S5 and S6). It is +0.09 only in S1 and S4, and -0.90 to -1.03 with any fps in the row. It adds no value in S2, so this test does not back it. If S1 or S4 were the expected column, it would pass by +0.09.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record [BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326], applied by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option: when the bill lands and what it does to cash and net debt, as numbers.
tests.numbers: Base free cash flow is $13.79B a year from 2030. Do Nothing: net debt $0 from end-2029 (2030 in stress). Re-engine: $5B over 2030-35, about $1.0B a year (7% of base FCF), booked at EIS, undiscounted debt penalty $0.6B. It returns $660M of PV per $1B of bill in S1-S3 and S6, and costs $496M per $1B in S4 and S5. Net debt $0 in base and stress. Rate: $2.94B evenly over 2030-32, $0.98B a year (7%). It returns +$31M per $1B in S1/S4 and costs $235-241M per $1B in the NGSA columns. Net debt $0 in base and stress. Both together: about $2B a year in 2030-32 (14%), net debt still $0. fps 10-year: $60.32B, peaking at 14% in year 7 = $8.4B (61% of base FCF); stress holds. fps 7-year: $65.00B, about $9.3B a year (67%); stress fails (peak $0.7B; $2.8B with the Re-engine). via Embraer: peak year about $14.0B, above base FCF; stress fails ($3.3-3.7B).

tests.name: fps site for the 2035 case: Renton or new site (inference; answers the CEO's ask 5)
tests.threshold: Renton only alongside a launch, with a MAX bridge and the rate step's wind-down planned; otherwise new_site.
tests.numbers: With fps on hold the site changes nothing; keep new_site. Alongside a launch, Renton is worth +0.44 to +0.62 (10-year) and +0.98 to +1.01 (7-year) on this grid, from about $3.0B of new-site capex avoided if chosen at least 3 years before EIS. The cost in operations: Renton's three MAX lines (47 of the 57 a month) wind down as the fps ramps, leaving the Everett North Line (up to 15 a month). The rate step rides on Renton too, which is why the rate with a Renton fps is -0.90 to -0.96. In real operations the wind-down must follow the fps's actual ramp, not its plan. An fps slip (doctrine prior +3 years) with the MAX already wound down would leave a delivery gap the board does not model. Decide in 2035, with a bridge plan.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (KPI veto NOT invoked)
vetoes.ground: The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, so the KPI doctrine gives me no ground for a veto this round. It would bind if such a problem were reported before the orders are sealed, and at execution the doctrine holds each step until KPIs and supplier output (LEAP-1B included) are stable. My hold recommendation rests on value (-0.69 in S2), not on KPIs. If the rate is ordered, its rationale must rest on production readiness and the visible backlog, not on Airbus (H6).

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag H4, not my veto: a 5-year overlap (fps 2030-37, Re-engine 2030-35), $3.0B of strain undiscounted, above the 2-year limit. The same breach applies to a Re-engine deferred to 2035 alongside a 2035 7-year fps.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_10yr with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: H4 flag, advice: a 2-year overlap (2033-35), $1.2B strain, exactly at the limit with no slack. A 2-year Re-engine slip (EIS 2037) would make the real engineering overlap 4 years. The grid also puts this row 3.18 to 4.52 below the Re-engine alone in every column.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice from the IP test, not binding: the partner adds no IP or capacity Boeing lacks on the board. It sits $18.05-18.06B below the 10-year Solo row in every column, with a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty, and stress-case net debt fails.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Rate Increase: a live quality escape, FAA scrutiny or supply-chain shortfall reported before the orders are sealed (including a LEAP-1B allocation or a fragile supplier short of about 65 a month) turns my KPI view into a binding veto. In the other direction, if Kelly holds S1 or S4 as the expected column and Jay shows the +0.09 survives our own 2035 fps plan, the capacity test passes and operations can deliver it, gated step by step. 787 Re-engine: I would move to hold on evidence of a supplier shortfall on its new parts, an engine durability gap at EIS, or a certification plan that needs production-certification concurrency. If an fps were added this round, a 10-year ramp sits at H4's 2-year limit and a 7-year breaches it. fps form: I would look at a partner only if one brought IP or capacity Boeing lacks at a cost within $1B of Solo, and on this grid none does.
ops.memo:
Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes, so the gates run on operations doctrine, marked as such.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery (record). The 737 delivered exactly to plan in 2026-29: 510, 594, 624, 654. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, so the KPI gate is open (doctrine) and my veto is not invoked. Operations can take +100 a year from 2032: 57 to 62, then about 65, each step after two to three stable months, at least six months apart, agreed with the FAA when we ask. That leaves up to a year of slack. Supplier readiness, LEAP-1B included, is a hard gate at every step.

Second, engineering capacity (doctrine). With fps on hold, strain is zero. A 2030 Re-engine runs 2030-35 and clears any 2035 fps. Deferred to 2035, it overlaps a 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B) or a 7-year by 5 ($3.0B, an H4 breach). Certify before building at rate.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth (record). Every $1B of Re-engine bill returns about $660 million in four columns and costs about $500 million in S4 and S5. Every $1B of rate bill returns $31 million at best, and costs $235 million in S2. Net debt holds at $0 in base and stress. Embraer adds no IP or capacity we lack, at $18B more.

Orders: fps hold; rate hold, on value, not KPIs; Re-engine launch if Kelly and the Board carry its market risk.

other_moves.move: Staged fps business case for the 2035 round (authority-to-offer work)
other_moves.detail: Solo by default. Compare the 7-year and 10-year ramps on the 2035 grid under the Board's rule: take the 10-year ramp only where it sits within $1B of the 7-year in every plausible column, otherwise the ramp with the higher worst column. Compare Renton with new sites, including a MAX bridge plan so the Renton wind-down follows the fps's actual ramp, not its plan. Carry Malave's risk-case column and the slip priors. Sequence the fps against any 787 Re-engine under H4. No date, no fixed-price development.

other_moves.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle
other_moves.detail: We invite all three narrowbody engine makers (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce) to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. Selection will be on value among engines actually launched, with proven durability before entry into service as a contract condition. No fps date and no launch commitment. This serves the dual- or triple-source engine enabler (unmet today). The engine code is decided at launch: code 3 (CFM) by default, or code 7 if P&W and Rolls-Royce can be ready by EIS.

other_moves.move: Keep 787 Re-engine readiness warm (study only, no launch)
other_moves.detail: Covers engineering definition, an engine-durability requirement with the engine makers, new-part supplier readiness (rate breaks only when supplier output is there, as on the 787 heat exchangers [B-2308]) and a certification plan with the type certificate before building at rate, so no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. Re-test it on the 2035 grid only if the A350 has not been re-engined (H3, second half). No programme spend committed.

other_moves.move: Hold the 737 at 57 a month with KPI gates and stability first
other_moves.detail: No rate step requested. KPIs are monitored monthly. Confirm the LEAP-1B allocation with CFM at today's rate, and keep the FAA-agreed process in place for any future step.

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot
other_moves.detail: Embedded staff, buffers and second sources where possible, so supplier readiness is never the reason a future programme slips.

other_moves.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
other_moves.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

other_moves.move: No shareholder-return signal
other_moves.detail: Net debt is at the historical level. Allocating the surplus cash is the Board's decision, so nothing is said publicly.

decision.public_statement:
When I came in, I said our priority, far and away, was debt, and that we'd do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing were ready. We've done the first part. The balance sheet is repaired, the 777X is delivering, the 737 MAX family is certified, and the 737 line is building steadily at 57 a month. A lot of people did hard work the right way to get here. I think we've turned the ship. Now the job is to keep it steady.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. The work on our next single-aisle goes on, in stages and with the data in front of us. We've asked all three engine makers to bring us their best proposals, with durability proven before entry into service. When we do launch, it will be on a conservative plan with headroom in it, and we will not take on fixed-price development risk.

On production, we'll keep the 737 where it is and keep it stable. A rate step only comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity. We'll keep adding 787 capacity in Charleston as our customers need it. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class. The financials will follow our production performance.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early. We'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever. fps hold (new_site, engine code null), rate_737 hold, re787 hold. Every field is at its default, so no item goes to the Board. The package below answers what it asked to see.

H1 AND H3 RULINGS FOR 2030 (management's call, with evidence)
- H1 (no fps in Round 1) is lifted because its 2026 grounds have lapsed. The 777X delivers from 2027 [BX-0550] and is cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547]. The MAX 7/10 certified in 2026 [BX-1299, BX-1873]. Net debt is $0.0B at end-2029 in the brief (end-2030 in stress, $3.3B at end-2029) [BX-1305, B-2327]. In July 2026 I put us about two years from financial readiness [BG-0068]. The grid, not the rule, holds the fps back.
- H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1): lifted on the same grounds. Its reason was the 777X first [B-2276].
- H3, second half, stays in force: no 787 Re-engine once the A350 Re-engine has launched. Nothing is on the record.
- Other rules: H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger. No certification trouble is reported, so the FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309]. H4, H5, H6 and H8 apply as written.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief reports no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The MAX delivered 510/594/624/654 to plan in 2026-29. Pope's KPI veto is not invoked.
2. Are market, technology and the balance sheet ready? The balance sheet is ready (net debt $0 in base and stress through 2050). Technology passes on the board. The market case is not ready: every fps row loses $2.08B to about $22B against Do Nothing in every column [BX-1296].
3. What if certification takes longer? Malave's buffer test (S6 against Do Nothing −0.02; the line is −2.02):
   - Fail (binding): every stand-alone fps row. The best, 10-year at Renton, is −3.47.
   - Pass: Do Nothing (0.00 gap), Re-engine (+3.28), Rate Increase (−0.71) and Rate Increase + Re-engine (+2.59).
4. Is this doing less, better? The Rate Increase sits within ε of Do Nothing in every column, so the smaller plan wins [BX-1239].

fps: HOLD
- Malave's veto binds on every 10-year, 7-year and via-Embraer row without the Re-engine. It also binds on 10-year + rate + Re-engine (−2.80; −2.22 at Renton, a narrow fail).
- Two fps rows pass his buffer: 10-year + Re-engine at Renton (−1.27) and at new sites (−1.78). Both sit 3.18 to 5.06 below the Re-engine alone in every column. Both are at H4's 2-year overlap limit with no slack, and the Board would veto both items.
- Via Embraer is about $18B worse than the Solo 10-year in every column, with a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty. Pope's IP test finds it adds nothing Boeing lacks.
- Objective premium for 50/50: $0. Chasing it costs at least $2.17B against the best plan in any column ($4.52B in S2), above the $2B cap.
- The future is built alongside the first three priorities [BX-1245]: a staged 2035 case (other move).

787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD (the hard call; I came in leaning to bring it)
- Item value: +3.30 in S1, S2, S3 and S6; −2.48 in S4 and S5.
- In my expected column, S2, it is the best plan by $3.30B, and it passes the buffer by $3.30B. Three things move me to hold.
- (a) The Board has said it will veto it under its −$1B per-item downside line, which counts every plausible column. The bulletin rules out no A350 Re-engine. Its veto binds and I have no override against it. Bringing an item I know will be vetoed is not proof before commitment [BG-0021].
- (b) Malave, my independent check [BX-1316], puts an A350 Re-engine this round at 40-50%.
  - The basis is company doctrine (profile §7): Airbus re-engines cheaply (the A330neo [B-2446]), expect an early attempt, and the widebody is a Chicken game.
  - Weighted, the edge is 3.30 − 5.78p = $0.41-0.99B, inside ε.
  - Inside ε, the higher worst column decides (Do Nothing −2.64 against −5.12 in S5), as do doing less [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548].
  - Doctrine, not my record, drove this probability read: I have no statement on Airbus's next airplane (Low), and Malave's seat is thin (Low).
- (c) My appetite for technology and launch risk is low; slow is fast [BX-1291].
- Cost logged separately as a Board-downside hold, not against the cap: $3.30B given up in S1, S2, S3 and S6; $2.48B saved in S4 and S5.
- Cost of waiting:
  - If the A350 moves first, H3 closes the Re-engine for good.
  - If not, a 2035 Re-engine (EIS 2040) overlaps a 2035 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B strain, at H4's limit) or a 7-year fps by 5 years (an H4 breach). The 2035 case must sequence them.
  - The 2035 grid will price this; I won't guess it.
- Pope's readiness results all pass (engineering free, Charleston, supplier gate, no concurrency). The programme is ready to bring once its market risk is acceptable.

737 RATE: HOLD
- Item value: −0.69 in S2 (expected); +0.09 only in S1 and S4; −0.69 to −0.71 in the NGSA columns.
- With any fps in the row it is −0.90 to −1.04 in every column. Its gain rests on nobody ever launching a new narrowbody, and our own plan carries a 2035 fps case.
- It lowers the worst column (S5 −3.34 against −2.64).
- The KPI gate is open. Pope says operations could deliver 57, then 62, then about 65 with slack, with the LEAP-1B allocation as a condition. FAA agreement would be sought step by step and has not been requested.
- This is a judgement on our own plan and production readiness, not on Airbus (H6).
- Doctrine's 'Rate Increase in Turn 1' (§6) rested on superseded engine numbers in which the rate added value alongside the fps. On this board that reverses (dashboard_game.md §5).
- The deferral is a loss we accept in S1 and S4 ($0.09B), not a wait.

ENGINE CODE AND SITE
- Engine code: null, since nothing is launched. At launch: code 3 by default, or code 7 if P&W and Rolls-Royce can be ready by EIS.
- Site: new_site. Renton changes nothing without a launch and is decided in 2035 with a MAX bridge plan.

BOARD PACKAGE
- Submitted row (Do Nothing): S1 +0.00 / S2 −0.02 / S3 −1.01 / S4 −2.62 / S5 −2.64 / S6 −0.02. No Board items, since each field is at its default.
- Expected column: S2. S6 is −0.02, 0.00 against Do Nothing. Buffer: pass. Fundable when the 777X turns: pass on timing.
- Net debt: $0 by end-2029 in base and end-2030 in stress, held to 2050.
- Premiums: soft $0 and objective $0. The Re-engine hold is logged separately, as above.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's binding veto struck every stand-alone fps row; none was ordered.
- Pope's KPI veto was not invoked.
- No overrides.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave's memo was the decisive input, weighed as my independent check [BX-1316]. His buffer veto binds; his other views are advice from a thin seat (one call, Low confidence).
- Buffer test: I accept it and his corrections. Two fps + Re-engine rows pass, not one. S6 is 4.55 below the Re-engine alone, not 4.52. 10-year Renton + rate + Re-engine fails narrowly at −2.22. No stand-alone fps row is ordered.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: I accept his pass on timing. The cash does not hold the fps back; the grid and the buffer do.
- Debt penalty: I accept that it is already netted and must not be subtracted again.
- Rate: I accept that its +0.09 cannot be shown to survive our own 2035 plan.
- What moved me was his 40-50% read of an A350 Re-engine this round. He drew it from company doctrine (§7), not his record. It puts the Re-engine's weighted edge ($0.41-0.99B) inside ε, where the higher worst column and doing less decide. Together with the Board's announced veto, that turned my lean to bring the Re-engine into a hold.
- I also log his offer: he would concur on the buffer if the Re-engine were brought, and he would change his mind on evidence the A350 stays put. That is the 2035 trigger.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope's seat runs on [NOW] operations doctrine with no airplane-business evidence (Very low confidence), so I weighed it as gates, not judgement.
- I accept her gate results: KPI gate open and her veto not invoked; zero strain with the fps on hold; a 2030 Re-engine clears any 2035 fps; via Embraer adds no IP or capacity; the Renton caveat that a MAX wind-down must follow the fps's actual ramp.
- Her rate path (57, then 62, then about 65, with up to a year of slack) and the LEAP-1B allocation condition go into the record. They show the hold rests on value, not readiness.
- Her Re-engine readiness results all pass. She recommended launching it if Kelly and the Board carry its market risk. The Board has said it will not carry that risk (−2.48 in S4/S5 breaks its −$1B line), and Malave's read puts the weighted edge inside ε. So I did not take her launch recommendation. Her readiness findings make it bringable in 2035 if the A350 has not moved.
- Her derivative slip prior (+2 years, unpriced) is noted for that case.

decision.expected_scenario: S2: Airbus launches NGSA, with the A350 not re-engined. The bulletin shows nothing launched, and Airbus was expected to fix its NGSA architecture around 2027 [B-2536]. S5 (NGSA + A350 Re-engine) is the plausible downside, at about 40-50% on company doctrine (§7, inference). S6, the risk case, equals S2 on every row without an fps. The column values our plan; it does not set our dates [B-2313].
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S2 the best plan is fps: hold + 787 Re-engine (+3.28). I chose fps: hold + 787: hold (−0.02), $3.30B below it. That is a Board-downside hold (the Board's −$1B per-item line, with its veto announced), logged separately and not against the cap. Probability-weighted at a 40-50% chance of an A350 Re-engine, the gap is $0.41-0.99B, inside ε.
decision.premium_reason:
Soft doctrine premium against the $2B cap: $0. Objective premium (50/50): $0, not chased; an fps now costs at least $2.17B against the best plan in any column, $4.52B in S2.
- fps hold: no premium. Hold beats the best fps row (10-year Renton, −3.44 in S2) by 3.42.
- Rate hold: no premium. Hold beats the Rate Increase by 0.69 in S2; I give up $0.09B in S1 and S4 only.
- 787 Re-engine hold: a known cost logged separately as a Board-downside hold, as the Board asked. It gives up $3.30B in S1, S2, S3 and S6 and saves $2.48B in S4 and S5. Probability-weighted at a 40-50% chance of an A350 Re-engine (doctrine), it costs $0.41-0.99B, which would fit inside the cap even if counted as soft.
- What breaks the number: if the A350 does not re-engine this round, the hold gives up the full $3.30B. Below a 39.8% chance, the hold stands only on the Board's line.
decision.objective_note:
The objectives never change the payoff.
- Hold the 50/50 split: unmet in every plan, and not chased, since the cost is above the cap.
- Defend incumbency: met on the brief's status quo, with NB share at 40.1% from 2030 while our factories, not demand, bind [BX-1293]. In the NGSA columns the share rule moves Airbus up 3 pp a year from NGSA EIS, so incumbency comes under pressure after about 2037. That is the case the staged 2035 fps must answer.
- Repair the balance sheet: met. Net debt is $0 by end-2029 (end-2030 in stress) and held to 2050 in base and stress on the chosen plan.
- Engine enabler (dual or triple sources; three NB makers): unmet, since only the 737 MAX on CFM flies. It is addressed by the unpriced, dateless public engine-sourcing requirement.
decision.predictions:
AIRBUS
- An NGSA launch this round is my expected case (S2).
- An A350 Re-engine attempt is about 40-50% on company doctrine (S4/S5), which is why the 787 Re-engine waits.
- Delay Tactics, if any, are covert and bite only from fps EIS. They cannot touch this round's plan: S6 equals S2 on every row without an fps.

ENGINE MAKERS
- No narrowbody engine launch keyed to Boeing this round, since no fps is live. Expect P&W and Rolls-Royce to follow NGSA's engine selection.
- CFM keeps the LEAP-1B on the 737 MAX.

OUR RESULTS THIS ROUND
- ΔPV: +0.00 S1, −0.02 S2, −1.01 S3, −2.62 S4, −2.64 S5, −0.02 S6.
- Net debt $0.0B in base and stress in every check year.
- NB delivered share 40.1% from 2030; WB share 58.8%.

2035
- Bring the staged fps case: Solo, the Board's ramp rule, Renton only with a bridge plan, and the risk-case column.
- Re-test the 787 Re-engine if the A350 has not re-engined, sequenced against the fps under H4.
- If NGSA launched in 2030 (EIS 2037), Airbus holds a lead edge for good. The 2035 grid, not the calendar, decides how we answer it.

airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft, for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. This is the Airbus of the 2030s that we have been preparing for: a step change in efficiency, built on technologies we have matured and demonstrated, the wing first among them, and on a production system designed together with the aircraft. We will invite CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to power it, so that our customers have a choice of engine and our ramp-up has secure supply. The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle offer. We will keep its lines running alongside the new aircraft's ramp-up, giving our customers a long and orderly transition. On widebodies our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. We will continue a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, and we are securing key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. The programme is funded from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
airbus.rationale:
DECISION. Launch NGSA in 2030, alone, on our own clock: EIS 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year, in the last year of the 2028-2030 window [AX-0020, AX-0006, A-0409]. The orders are engine code 7, the A320 Alt plan, the A350 Re-engine on hold and no Delay Tactics.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE ROWS (no PV trade-off).
(a) NGSA + A350 Re-engine on either A320 plan. Rule 6: two launches in one round, a 5-year overlap and $3B of strain. Peak cash is $6.67B a year against the $5.2B line, and the item is -2.15 in S6/S7. Both colleagues and the Board would veto it.
(b) Every Delay Tactics row. Rule 4: fps is not public. Rule 5: nothing is in development at order time. The naked fine is -15.74 in S1/S6, and the best gain is +0.29, below $1B. `bottleneck` and `both` also fail the integrity pillar.

STEP 2: SURVIVORS PASSING BOTH TESTS.

STEP 3: CHOOSE.

- Alt over base: +2.69 / +1.00 / +0.54 / +0.22 / +1.00 / +2.69 / +1.01. It never trails base.

- Alt also keeps the dual-source A320neo (CFM + GTF) building to about 2045, a hedge if NGSA slips, which Wagner names.

recommendations.text: Use the window: launch NGSA in 2030, its last launch year, for EIS 2037 on Airbus's own clock. Do not tie the timing to any expected Boeing move. Even in the worst column, S4, NGSA leads Do Nothing by +7.48 $B. Because this is a Qualified Majority launch, present the full S1-S7 row so that the finance and industrial directors are persuaded as well.

One programme at a time. Hold the A350 Re-engine until NGSA development spend rolls off. On current bills, a 2035 launch would overlap NGSA's last two development years (2035-36) at about $6.67B a year and fail the liquidity line, so bring the 2035 grid with the overlap and peak cash shown. If Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine, the A350 Re-engine stays on hold.

Take the A320 Alt plan only with the operating head's explicit confirmation that running the A320 lines at 82, 62, 52, 42 and then 14 a month alongside the NGSA ramp carries no safety, quality or supply-chain flag. Have the CFO show when the roughly $0.75B falls: if any of it falls before 2037, headroom under the $5.2B line is only about $0.02B.

Select NGSA engine code 7 (CFM plus P&W and Rolls-Royce). It names both makers whose conditional launches decide the stable-supply enabler: the brief shows 3 sources and 3 makers in 2050 if both launch when selected, and CFM alone otherwise. Code 7 also appears in no barred pair. The code never changes the payoff and is not a veto ground.

Read the whole row. The bulletin rules out no Boeing column. S4 (fps 7-yr entering service in 2037, the same year as NGSA) takes away the lead edge and the 60/40 objective, yet NGSA still earns +6.02 $B (+6.24 on the Alt plan) against -1.46 for Do Nothing. Present expected and worst columns side by side, and never cancel NGSA because of a Boeing move.
In public, give windows, not dates: entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. State support is upside only and must not be assumed in the case. Make no reference to Delay Tactics.
Confirm in the CFO's memo that on NGSA alone net cash and the A+/A1 rating hold, and that the 30-50% payout and the EUR 5bn buyback stay fundable without an equity raise or a dividend cut.

frame.asks_cfo:
Thomas, I need a memo in your "financial flexibility" register. Mark each test pass or fail for the default, the lean and the deleted rows.
1. Peak cash. NGSA at $35.52B / 7 = about $5.07B a year over 2030-36 against the $5.2B line (headroom about $0.13B). Show when the Alt plan's roughly $0.75B actually falls. If it falls after NGSA EIS in 2037, it should not touch the peak. If any of it falls in 2030-36, the total is about $5.18B and the headroom only about $0.02B: say whether that still passes in your judgement, and whether a one-year NGSA slip changes it.
2. Balance sheet. Confirm that on NGSA alone (and on NGSA plus Alt) net cash stays around $13.4B, the A+/A1 rating holds, and the 30-50% payout and the EUR 5bn buyback stay fundable with no equity raise and no dividend cut.
3. Robustness. Give a scenario table of the full S1-S7 rows for the default, the lean and Do Nothing; each Board item's row with its field at default; and the worst column. My working view is S2/S5 expected (fps 10-year or via Embraer, EIS 2040), S4 worst (fps 7-year, EIS 2037, the same year as NGSA), S1/S6 upside. Add your own scenario-weighted view, and say whether the Alt plan's margin over base (+2.69 / +1.00 / +0.54 / +0.22 / +1.00 / +2.69 / +1.01) is enough in your expected column to justify a second Board item.
4. Overlap. Confirm that NGSA + A350 Re-engine now fails: about $6.67B a year, two fronts, $3B strain, -2.15 in S6/S7. For the next round, show what a 2035 A350 Re-engine would do to peak cash in 2035-36, the last two NGSA development years, so the Board sees it before it is asked.
5. Delay Tactics. Confirm that every row fails the $1B test (at most +0.29) and record the naked-fine exposure (-15.74 in S1/S6), so the deletion is on file.
6. Board items. List each with its size and majority: NGSA $35.52B (Qualified Majority) and Alt plan about $0.75B. Draft the cash line of each Board-gate entry.
frame.asks_ops:
Lars, I need your production, quality and supply tests in writing. These are the results the Board will not let me override, so give each one an explicit pass or fail.
1. NGSA production readiness and engineering capacity. Is a 2030 launch, alone, compatible with holding the A320 at 85 a month to 2037 and with the A350F absorption, without competing for the same engineers and suppliers [A-0366, A-0485]? Flag any A320 ramp-shield or supply-crunch issue.
2. A320 Alt plan. Give an explicit safety, quality, ramp and supply-chain verdict on running the A320 lines at 82, 62, 52, 42 and then 14 a month for about eight years alongside the NGSA ramp (rate 50 about four years after EIS, 80 at six, 100 at eight). The Board approves Alt only with your clean confirmation. If you see any flag, base is our plan and I will not override you.
3. Engine code. You own the supply recommendation. The Board prefers code 7 (CFM + P&W + Rolls-Royce: in no barred pair, 3 sources and 3 makers in 2050 if both conditional engines launch, CFM alone otherwise). Tell me:
   - whether 7 is right, or whether 6 or 3 gives more supply certainty;
   - whether naming makers with no engine yet launched creates any quality or certification risk for a 2037 EIS (GTF2 would be ready around 2036, UltraFan NB around 2037);
   - whether the CFM fallback keeps EIS whole.
4. Supply security. Cover CFM capacity across both narrowbody lines in the overlap years. Tell me what we should secure in-house for the NGSA ramp (work packages, titanium, rare earths, the wing) as a public other move [AX-0054, AX-0060, AX-0061].
5. A350. Confirm Do Nothing on the A350 this round while the A350F matures and the widebody review runs [AX-0082, AX-0019], and give your view of a 2035 window.
6. Quality. Tell me if any order or public line we plan contradicts the five pillars.
frame.initial_lean:
My lean is to launch NGSA now, on our own clock, for entry into service in the second half of the next decade (EIS 2037). This is the last year of the window. Orders: `ngsa: launch`, `ngsa_engine_code: 7`, `rea350: hold`, `delay_tactics: none`, and `a320_plan: alt`, conditional on Wagner's clean safety, quality, ramp and supply result and on Toepfer showing that the $0.75B does not breach the $5.2B line. Otherwise `a320_plan: base`, the company default.

Grid for the lean: +13.71 / +10.08 / +10.38 / +6.24 / +10.08 / +12.85 / +9.22 in S1-S7. The worst column, S4, stays positive at +6.24, and against Do Nothing it gains +7.70 to +13.71 in every column. The default (base) row is +11.02 / +9.08 / +9.84 / +6.02 / +9.08 / +10.16 / +8.21.

S4 is the worst plausible column and S1/S6 the upside. The NGSA decision is the same in every column, so the scenario decides only base versus Alt. Alt never trails base, sits at the $1B line in S2/S5 and is below it in S3/S4, so it rests on my colleagues' tests, not on a premium.

The A350 Re-engine stays on hold: one programme at a time. A 2030 launch alongside NGSA breaks rule 6 and the peak-cash line and loses $2.15B in S6/S7; we revisit it in 2035 with the overlap shown.

Delay Tactics stay off, with no move this round: fps is not public, nothing of ours is in development, the move fails the $1B test and the team's stricter condition, and it sits against the integrity pillar.

Board items: `ngsa: launch`, the Qualified Majority item, shown with the full S1-S7 row and the Do Nothing row; and `a320_plan: alt` if chosen. I expect no override this round.

Public line: "Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do." Also a disciplined and controlled ramp, preparing the Airbus of the 2030s with entry into service in the second half of the next decade, and zero-for-zero trade.

Objective note: Defend 60/40 is likely lost in S4, and probably eroded after fps EIS in S2/S5, on any plan of ours. Code 7 is our best route to three engine makers, but it depends on P&W and Rolls-Royce. I will not trade PV for the objective.
