tests.name: Delay Tactics $1B test
tests.threshold: The move gains at least $1B over the same plan without it
tests.numbers: One move outside S1/S6: base -0.21 to -0.38; Alt +0.29 (S2/S5/S7), +0.01 (S3), +0.17 (S4); Do Nothing at most +0.24. Best case +0.29, below $1B. Both moves are negative in every column (base -0.76 to -16.25; Alt -0.26 to -16.25).

tests.name: Second move and five pillars: `both` and `bottleneck`
tests.threshold: Never a second move (`both` counts as two); no order the CFO, as chair of internal control, could not defend to the Audit Committee
tests.numbers: Two moves give the same 5 pp as one, so `both` adds $1B and buys nothing: -0.26 to -16.25 against no move on Alt. A covert supply-chain bottleneck beyond a first claim on scarce capacity cannot be defended under the integrity pillar. The Board vetoes `bottleneck` and `both` in any round.

tests.name: Poaching (rule 5)
tests.threshold: `poaching` only while NGSA or an A350 Re-engine is in development
tests.numbers: On the hold rows nothing is in development, so it fails. On the NGSA launch rows rule 5 would be met from 2030, but rule 4 (fps not public) and the $1B test (at most +0.29) bar it regardless.

tests.name: Delay Tactics cash
tests.threshold: Spread each $1B move evenly from the order year to fps EIS and add it to that year's spend
tests.numbers: No fps has been launched, so there is no EIS to spread over. No move is recommended. If one were ordered with NGSA, any amount above $0.13B in a year would break the $5.2B line.

tests.name: Board items (tie-break within $1B)
tests.threshold: Every order above EUR 300m is a Board item; within $1B, prefer fewer
tests.numbers: Default: 1 item, `ngsa: launch`, $35.52B booked at EIS (about EUR 32.3bn), Qualified Majority (above EUR 800m); the engine code rides with it. Lean: 2 items, adding `a320_plan: alt` at $0.75B (about EUR 0.68bn), Simple Majority. Alt's margin is not inside $1B in the expected column (+1.00) or equally weighted (+1.31), so the second item is justified, narrowly. It is inside $1B only in S3/S4 (+0.54 / +0.22). Draft cash line, NGSA: '$35.52B over 2030-36, about $5.07B a year against one year's FCF of about $5.2B, funded from operating cash flow with about $13.4B of net cash as buffer; no equity raise, no dividend cut.' Draft cash line, Alt: '$0.75B, budgeted from NGSA EIS in 2037 (about $0.09B a year), outside the 2030-36 peak; if any falls earlier, the peak is $5.18B, still inside the line.'

tests.name: Capex timing
tests.threshold: Between options within $1B, prefer the later capex start
tests.numbers: NGSA capex starts in 2030, the last launch year of the window (EIS 2037, rule 1), so no later start is available. The Alt cost is a post-EIS cost from 2037.

tests.name: Balance sheet: net cash, rating, payout and buyback
tests.threshold: No equity raise and no dividend cut; net cash (about $13.4B) kept as the buffer; 30-50% payout and EUR 5bn buyback stay fundable
tests.numbers: Net cash EUR 12,171m (about $13.4B); gross cash EUR 27,218m (about $29.9B). Peak programme spend sits inside one year's FCF, so no external funding is needed. The EUR 5bn buyback runs 2026-29, before NGSA's first development year. The 30-50% payout range gives room without a cut. Caveat: the record gives no FCF path for 2030-36. At FY2025 FCF, NGSA takes 97% of it (99% if the Alt cost falls in development), so the dividend in those years would come from FCF growth or from net cash. A+/A1: nothing here requires debt; the record does not give the agencies' thresholds. I re-test this in each budget cycle.

tests.name: Board downside: no Board item loses more than $2B against its default field in any plausible column
tests.threshold: Item value of -$2B or better in each of S1-S7
tests.numbers: NGSA item against Do Nothing: worst +7.48 (base), +7.70 (Alt). Alt item against base: worst +0.22. Deleted rows: the A350 Re-engine alongside NGSA is -2.15 in S6/S7 (fails); a Delay Tactics move is -15.74 in S1/S6 (fails).

tests.name: Cancel
tests.threshold: Cancel an A350 Re-engine only if a 787 Re-engine enters service first and the remaining spend loses at least $1B; never cancel NGSA
tests.numbers: Nothing has been launched; no write-off is possible.

vetoes.plan: `ngsa: launch` + `rea350: launch` on either `a320_plan` (both programmes launched in 2030)
vetoes.ground: Three failures. Peak cash: $6.67B a year in 2030-34 against the $5.2B line, $1.47B over. Rule 6 red line: a second new launch in the round, with a 5-year overlap and $3B of strain. Robustness: the added Re-engine is -2.15 in S6/S7, beyond the Board's $2B limit. Grid margin over the best passing option (the lean): +1.75 in S1-S5, -2.15 in S6/S7, so it is not ahead in the worst column. Because a red line is breached, no override can restore it.

vetoes.plan: Any `delay_tactics` this round (`bottleneck`, `poaching` or `both`) on any plan
vetoes.ground: Rule 4 red line: Boeing's fps is not on the public record, so a move is naked, costing -15.74 in S1/S6 (-16.25 for both). It fails the $1B test (best +0.29). `both` is a second move (red line), and `bottleneck`/`both` are flagged under the integrity pillar, which I could not defend to the Audit Committee. Margin over the best passing option: at most +0.29. Not overridable.

vetoes.plan: `ngsa: hold` + `rea350: launch`
vetoes.ground: Robustness fails: -0.64 against Do Nothing in S6/S7 (grid -1.50 / -2.01). This is a soft veto. It trails the best passing option (the lean) by $4.44B (S4) to $14.35B (S6) in every column, so no override can reach the $1B premium.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Alt to base: Wagner flags safety, quality, ramp or supply on the Alt plan. Or the $0.75B cannot be budgeted from 2037 and the NGSA bill carries an overrun above $0.13B (or the rate falls below $1.09 per EUR); in either case the lean breaks the $5.2B line. NGSA alone: a bill above $36.4B over 7 years (+$0.88B) would fail my peak-cash test. I would still expect an override to clear it (+7.48 over Do Nothing in S4), but it would have to be recorded as one. A350 Re-engine: a grid showing it at least $1B ahead of the best passing option in the expected column and ahead in the worst, with peak cash inside the line, or a Board decision. On current bills that means spend after 2036, because a 2035 launch peaks at $6.67B in 2035-36. Delay Tactics: only `poaching` alone, with Boeing's fps on the public record and not in service, NGSA in development, no earlier move, a gain of at least $1B in the expected column, and Faury's recorded decision setting aside the team's stricter condition.
cfo.memo:
Recommendation: launch NGSA alone with code 7 (Wagner's call), hold the A350 Re-engine, no Delay Tactics, and the A320 Alt plan if Wagner's result is clean.

Peak cash. NGSA is $35.52B over 2030-36: about $5.07B a year against one year's free cash flow of about $5.2B (EUR 4,753m at $1.10). Pass, with $0.13B of headroom. Alt's $0.75B buys A320 output after entry into service, so I would budget it from 2037 and leave the peak unchanged. If any of it falls in 2030-36, the peak is $5.18B: a pass, but within exchange-rate rounding. A one-year slip on the same bill cuts the annual spend to $4.44B. The risk is an overrun: $0.88B breaks the line.

Balance sheet. No equity raise and no dividend cut. The EUR 5bn buyback ends in 2029, before development starts, and about $13.4B of net cash is the buffer. The record gives no FCF path for 2030-36, so I re-test this in each budget cycle.

Robustness. In the worst column, S4, NGSA is +7.48 over Do Nothing (+7.70 on Alt). Alt adds +0.22 to +2.69: +1.00 in the expected column and +1.31 equally weighted. That just clears the bar for a second Board item.

Binding vetoes:
- NGSA with an A350 Re-engine: $6.67B a year, two launches, -2.15 in S6/S7.
- Any Delay Tactics: a naked fine of -15.74 against a gain of at most +0.29.
- An A350 Re-engine alone: -0.64 below Do Nothing in S6/S7.

A 2035 Re-engine would peak at $6.67B.

tests.name: Engineering capacity: NGSA alone (default and lean)
tests.threshold: NGSA and A350 development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain), unless the grid shows at least $1B more. Rule 6: at most one new launch per round
tests.numbers: NGSA develops 2030-2037 with rea350 on hold, so overlap is 0 years and strain $0. One launch this round. The A320 holds 85 a month (1,020 a year) through 2036 while NGSA is in development. The briefing constraint is NGSA and the A350 sharing teams, not NGSA against the A320 sustaining line. Talent binds both [A-0366, A-0485], and nothing here doubles the load.

tests.name: Engineering capacity: NGSA + A350 Re-engine in 2030 (deleted rows)
tests.threshold: Overlap of 2 years or less unless the grid shows at least $1B more; never two new launches in one round (rule 6, red line)
tests.numbers: NGSA develops 2030-37 and the A350 Re-engine 2030-35: a 5-year overlap and $3B strain ($3B x 5/5). That is two launches in one round. Against the best passing option (NGSA Alt + A350 hold) the premium is +1.75 in S1-S5 but -2.15 in S6 and S7 (on base: +1.74/+1.75 and -2.15). It is not $1B more in every plausible column. This is a red line, so no override is possible.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit absorption: default and lean (rea350 hold)
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed. Not in round 1 (2030); round 2 (2035) at the earliest
tests.numbers: rea350 hold. The widebody engineering stays on the A350F and the Spirit A350 packages, and the Board's widebody review runs on.

tests.name: A350F and Spirit absorption: any A350 Re-engine launch in 2030
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine in round 1 (company window 2033-35)
tests.numbers: NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine scores +3.26 / +2.75 / +3.28 / +1.80 / +2.75 / -1.50 / -2.01 (S1-S7). It trails the best passing option by 10.45 / 7.33 / 7.10 / 4.44 / 7.33 / 14.35 / 11.23, so no override can meet the $1B test. It also leaves NGSA's 2028-30 window. With NGSA alongside it, the rule 6 failure above also applies.

tests.name: Production readiness and rule 1 (NGSA launched 2030)
tests.threshold: Launch inside the 2028-2030 window, after the wing is proven buildable at rate and the production system has matured with the aircraft. No NGSA EIS before 2035 (rule 1, red line)
tests.numbers: Launch 2030, the last window year, gives EIS 2037, at or after 2035. The game proxy for the run-at-rate wing and production-system gates is met. This is a risk, not a fail: there is no schedule margin to 'around 2037', and a one-year slip lands in 2038. In public, give windows only.

tests.name: A320 ramp shield
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with an open A320 ramp commitment
tests.numbers: This board starts in 2030, after the end-2027 date of the inherited 70-75 commitment, and no ramp problem is reported. The A320 runs 85 a month (1,020 a year) through 2036 on both plans. NGSA takes no A320 slots before EIS 2037. Waiting backlog is 1,199 in 2030, peaks near 1,978 in 2033, and the firm backlog runs out by 2034. Hold the rate steady; do not push it.

tests.name: A320 Alt plan: safety, quality, ramp and supply verdict (ask 2)
tests.threshold: No safety, quality, ramp or supply-chain flag from running the A320 down from 82 a month alongside the NGSA ramp
tests.numbers: Alt runs the A320 at 82 / 62 / 52 / 42 / 14 a month over about 8 years; base runs 72 / 52 / 42 / 14 / none over about 5. Neither exceeds the 85 run since 2026. A320 engine demand at 82 a month is 984 aircraft and 1,968 engines (CFM about 1,181, P&W about 787), against 1,224 / 816 at 85. The NGSA ramp is the same on both plans. Alt adds about 1,500 A320s for about $0.75B. It keeps the dual-source A320neo (CFM + GTF) building to about 2045 instead of about 2042 (inference), a hedge against an NGSA slip. Alt minus base: +2.69 / +1.00 / +0.54 / +0.22 / +1.00 / +2.69 / +1.01. Conditions: the A320 steps are a ceiling and NGSA has first claim on resources. Re-check in 2035; the plan can change until EIS, so revert to base on a crunch, an engine slip or a quality event. Peak cash is Toepfer's test.

tests.name: Supply crunch
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch: no new concurrency
tests.numbers: No supply-chain crunch is reported in the round-1 bulletin or brief, and the board has no injects. The test is not triggered, and neither the default nor the lean adds concurrency.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If reported: re-time NGSA so EIS stays at or after the new technology-ready year; never cancel
tests.numbers: No slip is reported. NGSA EIS 2037 is after the 2035 technology-ready year.

tests.name: Engine supply: code 7 (recommendation, not a veto ground; ask 3)
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second maker (code 5, 6 or 7); code 7 when unsure which will be ready by NGSA EIS
tests.numbers: Readiness by EIS 2037: CFM is always ready (a LEAP derivative), so EIS stays whole and rule 8 cannot bind. P&W GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036 (1-year margin). RR UltraFan NB launched in 2030 is ready in 2037 (no margin). A Joint Venture formed in 2030 is ready in 2036. Launched in 2035 they would be ready in 2041 / 2042 / 2041, too late, so 2030 is the only round in which a second maker can reach 2037. In 2050 code 7 gives 1 source and 1 maker if the engine makers hold, and 3 and 3 if both launch when selected (Do Nothing: 2 and 2). Code 6 names only P&W and is barred if Boeing also picks 6. Code 3 locks in CFM alone. CFM already supplies about 2,592 narrowbody engines a year (A320neo 1,224 + MAX 1,368), so a CFM-only NGSA is a concentration risk. No certification or quality red flag: certify CFM first and the others as they mature, as on the A320neo (P&W November 2015, CFM May 2016).

tests.name: Supply security for the NGSA ramp (ask 4, public other move)
tests.threshold: Secure our own supply publicly for our own ramp, never as a claim on a rival's capacity (that would be a `bottleneck` move)
tests.numbers: Keep in-house: the NGSA wing (Wing of Tomorrow and the run-at-rate demonstrator) and aerostructures through Airbus Atlantic, Airbus Aerostructures and the ex-Spirit sites. Titanium and forgings: Aubert & Duval co-ownership and additive (DED) parts. Rare earths: the critical raw-materials watchlist. Engines: long-term capacity agreements with CFM covering the A320neo and NGSA from 2035, and second-source selection under code 7. All public; the board does not price them.

tests.name: Quality and the five pillars (ask 6)
tests.threshold: No order whose public explanation would contradict safety, quality, integrity, compliance or security
tests.numbers: The orders (ngsa launch, code 7, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt) and the planned line contradict no pillar. That line covers the five pillars, a disciplined and controlled ramp, EIS in the second half of the next decade and zero-for-zero. Keep 2037 and 85 a month out of public guidance; use windows.

tests.name: Delay Tactics (rules 4-5, integrity pillar)
tests.threshold: Only after fps is launched and before its EIS, at most one move (`both` is two), `poaching` only with a programme in development, `bottleneck` and `both` never
tests.numbers: fps is not launched (rule 4) and nothing is in development at order time (rule 5). `bottleneck` and `both` breach integrity. The lean plus one move, against the lean: -15.74 in S1 and S6 (the $48.32B naked fine) and at most +0.29 elsewhere, below $1B. The team's stricter condition cannot be met, because the move shifts share, not EIS.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: our own disciplined ramp
tests.numbers: No Rate Increase is on the public record. One would change none of our programmes.

tests.name: Engineering capacity: 2035 A350 Re-engine preview (ask 5, next round)
tests.threshold: Overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B), no crunch, no Boeing 787 Re-engine (rule 3)
tests.numbers: NGSA develops 2030-37 and a 2035 A350 Re-engine 2035-40: a 2-year overlap and $1.2B strain, exactly at my limit. It would pass my test only with NGSA on schedule, no crunch and no 787 Re-engine. If NGSA development ran a year longer, the overlap would be 3 years and $1.8B: fail. The Board puts 2035-36 peak cash at about $6.67B a year, which is Toepfer's test.

vetoes.plan: NGSA + A350 Re-engine in 2030, on either A320 plan (deleted rows)
vetoes.ground: Company red line rule 6: two new launches in one round, with a 5-year overlap and $3B strain. The grid premium over the best passing option (NGSA Alt + A350 hold) is +1.75 in S1-S5 but -2.15 in S6 and S7, not $1B more in every plausible column. It also fails the A350F and Spirit absorption test (no A350 Re-engine in round 1). A red line, so no override is possible.

vetoes.plan: NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine (the test to reject)
vetoes.ground: Fails the A350F and Spirit absorption test: no A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 packages are absorbed, so not in round 1 (2030). Soft veto. It trails the best passing option (NGSA Alt + A350 hold) by $4.44B (S4) to $14.35B (S6), so it can never be the $1B-better plan an override needs.

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics move (`bottleneck`, `poaching` or `both`) on any plan this round
vetoes.ground: Company red lines: rule 4 (fps is not launched or public) and rule 5 (no Airbus programme in development at order time). `bottleneck` and `both` also breach the integrity pillar. Naked-fine exposure is -15.74 in S1 and S6, with a gain of at most +0.29 elsewhere. No override possible.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Several things would change my view. If a later brief reports a supply-chain crunch, an engine maturity slip or an A320 or NGSA quality event, I revert a320_plan to base before NGSA enters service and add no concurrency; the A350 Re-engine stays on hold. If Toepfer shows that Alt's $0.75B breaks the $5.2B peak-cash line, base; that is his test and I accept it. If P&W and Rolls-Royce do not launch this round, code 7 still costs nothing but NGSA flies CFM alone, and that makes Alt's longer dual-source A320neo more valuable. On a 2035 A350 Re-engine, I pass it only at a 2-year overlap ($1.2B) with no crunch, no 787 Re-engine and NGSA on schedule. NGSA development finished, or a grid gain of at least $1B in every plausible column, would move me further. Nothing on this board moves me off NGSA in 2030 short of a reported failure of the wing or production-system gate.
ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived (Very low confidence): nothing of mine is on record, so I apply company doctrine.

NGSA in 2030, alone: pass. EIS 2037 clears the 2035 technology year, in the last launch year of the window. With the A350 Re-engine on hold, overlap and strain are zero. The A320 holds 85 a month to 2036; no open ramp commitment, supply crunch or quality event is reported. Schedule margin is thin: a one-year slip lands in 2038, so in public say "second half of the next decade", never a year.

Alt plan: clean. The A320 steps down from 82 and never exceeds the 85 it has run since 2026; its engine demand in the EIS year (about 1,180 LEAP, 790 GTF) stays below today's. It keeps a dual-sourced line running while NGSA ramps, a hedge if NGSA slips. Re-check in 2035 and revert to base on any crunch or quality event. Cash is Thomas's test.

Engine: code 7. CFM is always ready and keeps EIS whole. Only a 2030 selection lets a second maker reach 2037: GTF2 in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037 with no margin. Certify CFM first and the others after it, as on the A320neo.

Binding vetoes: any A350 Re-engine in 2030 (A350F and Spirit absorption; with NGSA, rule 6: 5-year overlap, $3B strain, -2.15 in S6/S7). Any Delay Tactics (rule 4; bottleneck and both breach integrity).

A 2035 A350 Re-engine would overlap 2 years at $1.2B of strain, which is my limit.

other_moves.move: Secure our own supply for the NGSA ramp
other_moves.detail: Keep the NGSA wing in-house: Wing of Tomorrow and the run-at-rate demonstrator, with aerostructures through Airbus Atlantic, Airbus Aerostructures and the ex-Spirit sites. Secure titanium and forgings through the Aubert & Duval co-ownership and additive (DED) parts. Extend the critical raw-materials and rare-earths watchlist to NGSA. This covers our own ramp only and makes no claim on any rival's capacity [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

other_moves.move: Multi-source engine strategy and long-term capacity agreements
other_moves.detail: Open NGSA propulsion to CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce (code 7). Seek long-term capacity agreements with CFM covering the A320neo and NGSA from 2035. Certify CFM first and further makers as their engines mature, as on the A320neo. The aim is supply certainty, not leverage [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

other_moves.move: Orderly A320neo family transition (Alt supply plan)
other_moves.detail: Keep the A320neo lines running longer alongside the NGSA ramp. The steps are a ceiling, never above today's rate, and NGSA has first claim on resources. The plan is re-checked at the 2035 gate and reverts to base on a supply crunch, an engine slip or a quality event. The cost is budgeted from NGSA entry into service.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
other_moves.detail: Work with the European and US industry associations, Boeing included, to keep civil aerospace on a tariff-free, zero-for-zero footing [AX-0088, AX-0046].

other_moves.move: Skills for the Airbus of the 2030s
other_moves.detail: Run apprenticeship, graduate and university programmes in Europe to grow NGSA engineering and production talent from our own pipeline. This is recruitment for the Airbus of the 2030s and targets no rival [AX-0073, A-0330].

other_moves.move: 2035 gate review (internal)
other_moves.detail: Hold a Board and ExCo gate in 2035 covering three questions. First, NGSA technology and production-system maturity and schedule margin, since a one-year slip lands in 2038. Second, whether the Alt plan should stand or revert to base. Third, the A350 Re-engine test with full overlap and peak cash: Toepfer's preview shows $6.67B a year in 2035-36, which fails the $5.2B line unless spend starts after 2036, and rule 3 applies if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine.

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Today Airbus launches its next-generation single-aisle aircraft, for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. This is the Airbus of the 2030s that we have been preparing for: a step change in efficiency, built on technologies we have matured and demonstrated, the wing first among them, and on a production system designed together with the aircraft. We will invite CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to power it, so that our customers have a choice of engine and our ramp-up has secure supply. The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle offer. We will keep its lines running alongside the new aircraft's ramp-up, giving our customers a long and orderly transition. On widebodies our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. We will continue a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, and we are securing key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. The programme is funded from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
DECISION. Launch NGSA in 2030, alone, on our own clock: EIS 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year, in the last year of the 2028-2030 window [AX-0020, AX-0006, A-0409]. The orders are engine code 7, the A320 Alt plan, the A350 Re-engine on hold and no Delay Tactics.

STEP 1: DELETE RED-LINE ROWS (no PV trade-off).
(a) NGSA + A350 Re-engine on either A320 plan. Rule 6: two launches in one round, a 5-year overlap and $3B of strain. Peak cash is $6.67B a year against the $5.2B line, and the item is -2.15 in S6/S7. Both colleagues and the Board would veto it.
(b) Every Delay Tactics row. Rule 4: fps is not public. Rule 5: nothing is in development at order time. The naked fine is -15.74 in S1/S6, and the best gain is +0.29, below $1B. `bottleneck` and `both` also fail the integrity pillar.

STEP 2: SURVIVORS PASSING BOTH TESTS.
- NGSA base (company default): +11.02 / +9.08 / +9.84 / +6.02 / +9.08 / +10.16 / +8.21.
- NGSA Alt: +13.71 / +10.08 / +10.38 / +6.24 / +10.08 / +12.85 / +9.22.
- Do Nothing: 0.00 / -0.51 / +0.02 / -1.46 / -0.51 / -0.86 / -1.37. A hold, never vetoed, but it closes the window.
NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine fails Toepfer's robustness test (-0.64 against Do Nothing in S6/S7) and Wagner's A350F absorption test. It trails Alt by $4.44-14.35B, so no override can reach it.

STEP 3: CHOOSE.
- NGSA launch over Do Nothing: +7.48 to +11.02 in every column on base. The decision is the same in every Boeing column.
- Alt over base: +2.69 / +1.00 / +0.54 / +0.22 / +1.00 / +2.69 / +1.01. It never trails base.
- In my modal Boeing outcome (fps entering service in 2040, S2/S5) the margin sits exactly on the $1B line. The cells are rounded to 0.01, so I do not rest the choice on that single cell.
- Scenario-weighted, the margin is +1.47 on my weights and +1.31 equally weighted. Both are above the $1B doctrine threshold, so the default is not 'within $1B' and the highest-grid survivor carries.
- Tie-breaks would favour base only inside $1B (fewer Board items, less concurrency); they do not apply here.
- Alt also keeps the dual-source A320neo (CFM + GTF) building to about 2045, a hedge if NGSA slips, which Wagner names.
- Robustness: the worst column, S4, stays positive at +6.24 (+7.70 against Do Nothing). No Board item loses more than $2B in any column.

STEP 4: VETO CHECKS.
- Toepfer: three binding vetoes, all on deleted rows (NGSA + A350 Re-engine; any Delay Tactics; NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine). I accept all three.
- Wagner: three binding vetoes on the same deleted rows. I accept them.
- Neither colleague vetoes the chosen plan. No override is used; the game's single override stays unspent.

ENGINE CODE 7. This is Wagner's supply recommendation and the Board's preference. 2030 is the only round in which a second maker can reach a 2037 EIS (GTF2 ready 2036; UltraFan NB ready 2037, with no margin). CFM is always ready, so EIS stays whole and rule 8 cannot bind. Code 7 is in no barred pair. It has no payoff effect.

DELAY TACTICS. None proposed, so the team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) stays in force as the default. I record no decision to set it aside.

BOARD-GATE LINES.

   - Five pillars: pass. On the technology clock, no pillar flag (Wagner).

recommendations.text: Put NGSA on the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review: wing and production-system maturity, and the A320 run-down under the Alt plan. Schedule margin is thin, since a one-year slip lands EIS in 2038. Revert the Alt plan to base before EIS on any supply crunch, engine slip or quality event, as the operating head conditions it. Never re-time NGSA ahead of its technology clock.

Keep engine code 7 to EIS. In 2035 the operating head should report whether P&W and Rolls-Royce launched on selection. If neither did, NGSA flies CFM alone: 1 source in 2050, against 2 today. The longer CFM + GTF A320neo run under the Alt plan then becomes the supply hedge, and the CFM capacity agreement the priority. The code never changes the payoff and is not a veto ground.

On the other moves (below the threshold; recommendation only), the Board endorses three: securing Airbus's own supply, zero-for-zero advocacy and the internal 2035 gate. Two need limits:
- CFM long-term capacity agreements: confine them to Airbus's own A320neo and NGSA volumes, with no exclusivity and nothing above its own ramp.
- Skills programme: draw from Airbus's own pipeline, with no targeted hiring from a rival's fps team.
Ask the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee to review both so that neither can be read as a Delay Tactics move.

The public statement is acceptable. It gives windows, not dates ('second half of the 2030s'), and the Board endorses the correction. It names no rate or plan target and does not mention Delay Tactics. On 'preserving ... our shareholder return policy': NGSA takes about 97% of FY2025 FCF. The CFO should therefore confirm each cycle that the 30-50% payout stays fundable from FCF and net cash. Any new buyback comes to the Board as a reserved matter with the NGSA peak shown. State support remains upside only.

Reaction discipline and Delay Tactics.
- NGSA: never cancel it on a Boeing move. Even in S4, the worst column, it leads Do Nothing by +7.70. The Board would veto a cancellation unless continuing loses at least $1B in every plausible column.
- Delay Tactics: keep them off. `bottleneck` and `both` are vetoed in any round. `poaching` comes to the Board only if every condition holds: fps is public and not in service, NGSA is in development, there has been no earlier move, the gain is at least $1B in the expected column, the CEO records setting aside the team's stricter condition, and the public statement is silent on it. On this grid the best gain is +0.29.

Under the brief's share rules, Defend 60/40 is likely to erode after fps EIS in S2-S5 and S7, and no order on this board restores it. Do not trade PV, integrity or the balance sheet for it. The game's single override remains unspent; reserve it.

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run 2030, and every year after.

Here's what we know. Our airframer customers are working on their next narrowbody plans. What they launch, and when, is their call, not ours. Whatever they launch, CFM will offer an engine for it, and we're working closely with both of them, privately, on what that aircraft needs. We don't have a birthright on that next order, and we won't act like we do.

RISE stays fully funded as our technology programme with our partners at Safran, and testing goes on. We won't put an entry-into-service date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it, and on what we know today that is 2045 at the earliest. Meanwhile, what we learn there keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet.

On the widebody, we're investing in the GEnx for our 787 customers.

Here's what we don't know: which aircraft launch, when, and with what engines. When we know, you'll know. Until then we keep getting after LEAP durability and deliveries with our supply base. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW DO WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base on whatever new narrowbody gets launched, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. Nothing is launched yet and no rival engine is on the record. Both airframers have published production plans that kick in once they launch. CFM is always fitted, at worst on a LEAP derivative. But S3 (-32.59) and S6 (-57.46) show what a rival-only selection costs us, and nothing on this round's grid wins that slot back. We win this round by banking what pays in every column, keeping RISE whole and keeping our powder dry for the round when selections are public. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

DECISION: genx upgrade_genx9. Hold ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. This is option B, the plan all three of us arrived at on our own.

- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]: GEnx is +0.78 in S1, S3, S4, S5 and S6 and +0.77 in S2, with no R&D, no strain and no downside. It defends the 787 on product: 15% better fuel burn and best-in-class time on wing, wins that weren't about price [CX-0615, CX-0599].
- The Ducted's S1 cost is its whole $4B bill (-4.00), and S6 is also -4.00. It pays only where an airframer puts us next to a rival (S2 +1.50, S5 +5.28), and those selections aren't on the record.
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: my weights are S1 10%, S2-S6 18% each, tilted toward a launch with unknown selections. On those weights: GEnx alone -26.31; the package (Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx) -26.87; Do Nothing -27.09; Ducted alone -27.10. At equal weights: -24.30 / -25.27 / -25.08 / -25.39. GEnx alone is best either way.
- Break-even weight on S5: the Ducted needs about 21%; the package about 28%; clearing the Board's $1B margin needs about 36%-40%. Nothing on the record gives me that.
- Tie-break [CX-0658]: the package sits 0.56 behind GEnx alone, inside my $1B ε, so safety, quality, delivery and cost decide. One project puts nothing new on a supply base still working off LEAP durability and the ramp (safety and quality). It doesn't pull engineers or supplier slots off LEAP deliveries (delivery). It carries no $4B-$6B bill (cost). GEnx alone wins all four.
- No birthright [CX-0564]: I read S3 and S6 as hard as S2 and S5. In S3 and S6 the Ducted loses (-1.25, -4.00) and wins nothing back.
- H3: the trigger is met only through the grid's S3 and S6. No rival narrowbody engine has been launched, committed or selected. A Ducted is a defence, and on this board it doesn't defend the columns where we'd need it. So hold, re-test in 2035.
- Staging: the grid can't price it, and I won't pretend it can. Waiting gives up the early +10 pp ramp years in S2 and S5 (2037-2040 on an NGSA) and saves the full $4B in S1, S3 and S6. Ali confirms a 2035 Ducted is ready in 2041, and that a late Ducted still earns from its ready year. Launching now and cancelling later writes off $3.33B.
- The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]: every airframe column puts a new narrowbody in service in 2037-2040, before a 2045 Open Fan. The Open Fan item runs -8.00 to -34.29, or -11.00 to -29.57 with Lobby. That's far above the $2.0B cap and outside the RISE allowance, which can't carry a wait penalty in plausible columns. A 2035 launch is ready in the same year for the same $8B. Hold, no cancel (H5).
- Lobby (-1.00, or -3.00 with strain) and Partner Embraer have no engine to serve. Here doctrine drove the hold, not my record: I have no evidence on Embraer or on lobbying.
- Can the suppliers carry it: one project, no $2B strain. Ali found no supply case on the floor, so I followed doctrine.
- Next generation: my 20% line binds RISE. No Ducted is launched, so it isn't engaged. If one comes in 2035, it's a defensive LEAP-class step, never the next generation [CX-0217, CX-0183, CX-0208].

RED LINES
- H1: CFM offers an engine for any new narrowbody.
- H2: no Open Fan.
- H3: no Ducted without a defence case.
- H5: RISE funded.
- H7: no CFM narrowbody order this round, so no Safran consent is needed. GEnx is GE alone. The public engine offer and RISE-as-technology fit joint practice, so consent is assumed (inference).
- H8: no rival named.
- H9: premium $0.
- Ali: no safety or durability flag.
Ghai's and Ali's vetoes covered C, D, F, Lobby, stacking and Partner Embraer on an Open Fan. None is ordered, so there are no overrides.

FOLLOW THE RECORD OR DOCTRINE: GEnx (inference from CX-0615 and CX-0599), Ducted timing (my call), Partner Embraer and Lobby (doctrine), and Open Fan and RISE (record plus H2 and H5).

frame.question: What game are we playing, and how do we win? The game is the installed base on whichever new narrowbody launches this round. It is not share for its own sake [CX-0467, CX-0422, CX-0493]. There are two open slots. An NGSA launched now enters service in 2037. An fps enters in 2037 on the 7-year ramp or 2040 on the 10-year. On this board CFM is always fitted, at worst on a LEAP derivative. But we don't have a birthright on that next order [CX-0564]. S3 and S6 show what a rival selection does to us (-32.59 and -57.46), and nothing we can order this round buys that slot back. So the round comes down to one question. Do we pay $4B now for a Ducted that earns money only where an airframer puts us next to a rival (S2 +1.50, S5 +5.28), before any selection is on the record? Or do we take the dollars that are there in every column (GEnx, +0.77 to +0.78), keep RISE whole as technology, and stage the Ducted until the airframers have chosen? We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630]. We win by banking what pays in every column we can see and by planning on the record, not on the hope of orders not yet won [CX-0248].

My lean, before the memos: genx: upgrade_genx9 alone, and hold on ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. That is option B.

Why:
- GEnx is the one move that pays in every column we can see: +0.78, with no R&D, no strain and no downside. It defends the 787 on product, GE alone [CX-0615, CX-0599].
- The public record shows no airframe launched and no rival engine. So I weigh the six columns about equally for now. I won't book S5 because I hope for it [CX-0248, CX-0536]. On those weights GEnx alone (-24.30) beats Do Nothing (-25.08), the package (-25.27) and the Ducted alone (-25.39). I'll book expected PV low.
- The Ducted pays only where an airframer puts us next to a rival (S2, S5). It loses its whole bill in S1 and S6 and wins nothing back in S3. On this board a 2035 launch (ready 2041) risks years of gain, not the slot.
- One project at a time, in keeping with lean before capital.

Open Fan: hold. Every airframe column enters service before 2045 (H2), and a 2035 launch is ready in the same year. RISE stays whole as technology, with no cancel (H5). The Open Fan objective is likely missed if an airframe launches now. I'll say so in dollars and not pay a premium to dress it up. The RISE allowance stays unused.

Lobby and Partner Embraer: hold. Neither has an engine to serve.

What changes my mind:
- a credible read that S5 or S2 carries more than about 21% of the weight (28% for the package);
- Rahul's numbers showing the Ducted paid for;
- Mohamed confirming 2036 on test evidence with no flag.
Within $1B, safety, quality, delivery and cost decide, in that order.

Safran gate:
- GEnx is GE alone.
- Any Ducted needs my sentence: a competitive CFM engine offered to both airframers where a rival may share the slot. Consent is assumed on that reason (inference).
- Partner Embraer and Lobby are joint; consent assumed (inference).

Public line, in draft: CFM will offer both airframers a CFM engine on any new narrowbody; RISE is technology until an airframer wants it, with entry into service at 2045 at the earliest; we name no one. Tell you what we know, tell you what we don't. It ain't that hard.

If 'competitive' reaches public text as a price claim, it trips this test and needs Safran.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
I would pass a Ducted on any of these: (1) An airframer launches and selects CFM next to a rival on the public record (code 6 or 7). That makes S2 or S5 a record column, where the Ducted is +1.50 or +5.28, and I would pass a 2035 Ducted on that round's grid. (2) A rival narrowbody engine is launched, committed or selected on the record, and the grid shows the Ducted beating hold in that column. (3) Culp brings evidence from the record, not hope, that puts S5 at 21% of the weight or more for the Ducted alone, or 28% for the package (36% and 40% to clear the Board's $1B margin). (4) A later grid that prices the staged Ducted shows the 2037-2040 ramp years worth more than the $4B it saves in S1, S3 and S6.

On the Open Fan: an airframer commits to a narrowbody whose first entry into service is no earlier than 2045, with the declared premium inside the RISE allowance.

On GEnx: a re-engine or a rival widebody upgrade on the record would make me re-test the +0.78.
cfo.memo:
Larry, there's nothing to hide here. One move pays in every column: the GEnx upgrade, +0.78 in S1 through S6 (+0.77 in S2), with no R&D, no strain and GE alone. Its gain starts in 2042 on this board. I pass it.

The Ducted doesn't pass. Its $4B pays only in S2 (+1.50) and S5 (+5.28), and both assume a selection nobody has made. We need to work the volumes with the airframers before we put a number on it. Through the hard-rule-3 carve-out it is judged where a rival takes our slot, and there it loses: -1.25 in S3, -4.00 in S6. At equal weights it is -0.31 against hold, and -0.96 inside the package. To clear the Board's $1B it needs S5 at 36% of the weight. The Open Fan's $17.8B premium is above the cap and the RISE allowance. Lobby alone is -1.00.

Capex isn't the constraint. A Ducted with strain is about $1.0B a year against $2.5B of room after 70% of $8.5B goes back. No rating risk.

What the case leaves out: S6 at -56.68, 32 below our -24.30. But that is hold's exposure, not GEnx's. Rivals can still move after this round, and no widebody move is in these columns.

Staging gives up the early ramp years in S2 and S5 and saves $4B in S1, S3 and S6. I won't price what the grid can't.

Book it low, about -26, and take no S1 upside until the selections are public.

Conditions if Culp launches: (1) never call it the next generation; a ducted engine gets less than half the open fan's fuel-burn gain, so Culp's 20% line binds RISE, not this defensive step; (2) no ready year before 2036 in any statement; (3) durability and the ready date are owned by a cross-functional team, with turn on, turn off before any date moves. ops.would_change_mind_if: Test or field data only, never analysis. (1) Ducted: if Culp puts a rival new narrowbody engine on the record as launched, committed or selected (the hard-rule-3 trigger is his call), I need only a durability plan for the hot section, cross-functionally owned, that holds 2036 or later. Then I have no objection to a launch at launch + 6. (2) Open Fan: nothing on this board moves 2045 earlier. I would back a 2035 launch only on two conditions: the public record shows that no new narrowbody can enter service before 2045, and RISE ground and flight tests with Safran and Airbus show no open durability failure (dust, hot-and-harsh). (3) Stacking: field data showing the 9 suppliers at 15 sites delivering the LEAP rate with margin. (4) Any test or field result showing a durability shortfall on an engine we order raises a flag that the Board must see resolved cross-functionally.
ops.memo:
Turn on, turn off. I tested every date against the board's development times.

Ducted: launched now, ready in 2036, launch plus 6. That is one year before an NGSA or a 7-year fps (2037) and four before a 10-year fps (2040). The date passes. But it is a schedule, not a test result: nothing unlaunched has been tested. 2036 is the floor; I accept no earlier date. I see no safety or durability flag on the evidence. And the physics: a ducted engine gets less than half the open fan's fuel-burn gain. It is a defensive step in the LEAP class, never the next generation. Staged to 2035, it is ready in 2041: four years late on an NGSA, one on a 10-year fps.

Open Fan: ready in 2045, launched now or in 2035. Every airframe column enters service first, by 8 years on an NGSA and 5 on a 10-year fps. Hold. A 2035 launch is the last that can be ready by 2050.

GEnx: an upgrade on a proven architecture. Ready in 2033, it counts from 2035 at the earliest, or 2042 if nobody re-engines. One project, no strain. I favour it.

No date veto as framed. Partner Embraer on an Open Fan would fail: it counts from 2037 on an engine ready in 2045.

Supply: my record is silent, so I follow doctrine: one project unless the grid pays the strain.

We failed twice. We got it done. RISE stays whole.

other_moves.move: Offer a CFM engine for any new narrowbody either airframer launches, at minimum a LEAP derivative
other_moves.detail: H1: we never refuse an airframer and never lock one out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. This is a product offer only, with no price, terms or concession [CX-0184]. It is what CFM does today on the 737 MAX and A320neo, so it fits joint practice and Safran's consent is assumed (inference). The board does not price it.

other_moves.move: RISE stays funded as a technology programme with Safran: ground, durability and dust testing continue; no product launch and no entry-into-service date
other_moves.detail: H5: no cancel, and no programme dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398]. RISE becomes a product when an airframer wants it [CX-0469, CX-0205]. RISE is a joint programme with Safran, and continuing it as technology is joint practice. Ali's floor applies: no Open Fan before 2045, and that is a floor, not a promise. RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades [CX-0162].

other_moves.move: Private product and technology-roadmap talks with both airframers on their next narrowbody
other_moves.detail: Talks on platforms stay private [CX-0586]. We want to be on all the critical platforms [CX-0587]. The goal is to learn requirements and timing first-hand, not to sell a date.

other_moves.move: Ducted decision staged to the 2035 round
other_moves.detail: No money committed and no date given. It gets re-tested on the 2035 grid if any of these lands on the record: an airframer selection that puts CFM next to a rival (an S2- or S5-type column); a rival new narrowbody engine launched, committed or selected (H3); or a 2035 grid showing the Ducted ahead of hold by more than $1B. Ali's conditions carry over: a cross-functional durability plan for the hot section, no ready year before launch + 6, and the Ducted is never called the next generation.

other_moves.move: LEAP durability kits and supply-base work (FLIGHT DECK) continue ahead of any new programme
other_moves.detail: Safety, quality, delivery, cost [CX-0658]. 80% of shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613]. We fix the supply base we have before we load it with a new programme (lean before capital) [CX-0540, CX-0653].

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run 2030, and every year after.

Here's what we know. Our airframer customers are working on their next narrowbody plans. What they launch, and when, is their call, not ours. Whatever they launch, CFM will offer an engine for it, and we're working closely with both of them, privately, on what that aircraft needs. We don't have a birthright on that next order, and we won't act like we do.

RISE stays fully funded as our technology programme with our partners at Safran, and testing goes on. We won't put an entry-into-service date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it, and on what we know today that is 2045 at the earliest. Meanwhile, what we learn there keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet.

On the widebody, we're investing in the GEnx for our 787 customers.

Here's what we don't know: which aircraft launch, when, and with what engines. When we know, you'll know. Until then we keep getting after LEAP durability and deliveries with our supply base. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW DO WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base on whatever new narrowbody gets launched, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. Nothing is launched yet and no rival engine is on the record. Both airframers have published production plans that kick in once they launch. CFM is always fitted, at worst on a LEAP derivative. But S3 (-32.59) and S6 (-57.46) show what a rival-only selection costs us, and nothing on this round's grid wins that slot back. We win this round by banking what pays in every column, keeping RISE whole and keeping our powder dry for the round when selections are public. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

DECISION: genx upgrade_genx9. Hold ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. This is option B, the plan all three of us arrived at on our own.

THE TESTS
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]: GEnx is +0.78 in S1, S3, S4, S5 and S6 and +0.77 in S2, with no R&D, no strain and no downside. It defends the 787 on product: 15% better fuel burn and best-in-class time on wing, wins that weren't about price [CX-0615, CX-0599].
- The Ducted's S1 cost is its whole $4B bill (-4.00), and S6 is also -4.00. It pays only where an airframer puts us next to a rival (S2 +1.50, S5 +5.28), and those selections aren't on the record.
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: my weights are S1 10%, S2-S6 18% each, tilted toward a launch with unknown selections. On those weights: GEnx alone -26.31; the package (Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx) -26.87; Do Nothing -27.09; Ducted alone -27.10. At equal weights: -24.30 / -25.27 / -25.08 / -25.39. GEnx alone is best either way.
- Break-even weight on S5: the Ducted needs about 21%; the package about 28%; clearing the Board's $1B margin needs about 36%-40%. Nothing on the record gives me that.
- Tie-break [CX-0658]: the package sits 0.56 behind GEnx alone, inside my $1B ε, so safety, quality, delivery and cost decide. One project puts nothing new on a supply base still working off LEAP durability and the ramp (safety and quality). It doesn't pull engineers or supplier slots off LEAP deliveries (delivery). It carries no $4B-$6B bill (cost). GEnx alone wins all four.
- No birthright [CX-0564]: I read S3 and S6 as hard as S2 and S5. In S3 and S6 the Ducted loses (-1.25, -4.00) and wins nothing back.
- H3: the trigger is met only through the grid's S3 and S6. No rival narrowbody engine has been launched, committed or selected. A Ducted is a defence, and on this board it doesn't defend the columns where we'd need it. So hold, re-test in 2035.
- Staging: the grid can't price it, and I won't pretend it can. Waiting gives up the early +10 pp ramp years in S2 and S5 (2037-2040 on an NGSA) and saves the full $4B in S1, S3 and S6. Ali confirms a 2035 Ducted is ready in 2041, and that a late Ducted still earns from its ready year. Launching now and cancelling later writes off $3.33B.
- The airframer sets the date (H2) [CX-0205, CX-0469]: every airframe column puts a new narrowbody in service in 2037-2040, before a 2045 Open Fan. The Open Fan item runs -8.00 to -34.29, or -11.00 to -29.57 with Lobby. That's far above the $2.0B cap and outside the RISE allowance, which can't carry a wait penalty in plausible columns. A 2035 launch is ready in the same year for the same $8B. Hold, no cancel (H5).
- Lobby (-1.00, or -3.00 with strain) and Partner Embraer have no engine to serve. Here doctrine drove the hold, not my record: I have no evidence on Embraer or on lobbying.

pratt_whitney.public_statement: Bad news first. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has slipped from 26.7% in 2026 to 24.4% in 2029 as the market mix moved, though we still deliver our full share of the A320neo. We control what we can control. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it, as sole or shared source, provided GTF2 can be ready by that airframe's entry into service. GTF2 is ready six years from launch, so a launch this year is ready in 2036. It will not enter service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. It builds on the durability work we are doing on the GTF fleet today. The offer is on standard terms, with no launch discounts; these are responsible bets with responsible paybacks. We are not committing to a Joint Venture today. We will consider one only once a partner's commitment, or an airframer's demand for one, is on the record, and any partnership will share risk and investment, never our core technology. The airframers will speak for their own programmes. The dividend comes first, and this plan needs no change to it or to our path on debt.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
EXCO DELIBERATION, ROUND 1 (2030). Decided by the team rule.

1. Starting point: Eddy's proposal, gtf2_solo launch_if_selected and jv_with_rr hold. Mitchill recommends the same orders, so both memos and the Board's guidance converge on Option A.

2. Binding vetoes struck:
- Mitchill, ground 2 (carrying an unselected engine), binding: the unconditional launch (C and F). Its edge over launch_if_selected is -0.73 at his weights, -0.64 at the Board's and -0.64 at my final weights. It is still about -0.5 with the 2035 cancel written in at a $1.67B write-off. Break-even needs p(S6) at 0.585 of the S1+S6+S7 mass; I have 0.10 of 0.50 = 0.20. It also fails the Board's +$0.5B bar. No objective premium buys a hedge that fails ground 2.
- Mitchill, ground 4 (booking unproven upside), binding: the Joint Venture commitment (D, E and F). Rolls-Royce has no commitment on the record and no live code includes Rolls-Royce. Committing is -2.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere, a weighted -0.20.
- Eddy: no binding veto on any option. His readiness check passes.
- Board: it vetoes the same two items, and approves launch_if_selected or hold.
- I accept every veto and revise nothing, because A carries no veto. 'overrides' is empty.

3. The safety and durability constraint, set first [PX-0035][PX-0073]:
- A 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036. EIS is 2037 for NGSA and the 7-year fps (one year of margin) and 2040 for the 10-year and Embraer fps (four years).
- launch_if_selected cannot fire into an airframe GTF2 cannot serve.
- My own operating dates have slipped, by about two years on the Advantage [PX-0017][PX-0087], so I discount them. That is why the public line promises 'ready six years from launch' and not a 2037 entry into service.
- The binding condition, as Eddy wrote it: durability proven, every life-limited part at full life, no compressed testing. If the data are not in, the EIS moves.

4. Optimising inside the constraint. Option A has the best expected PV of A to F at every weight set tested:

| Weights | A | Hold (B) | C (unconditional launch) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Mine (final) | +0.96 | -8.17 | +0.31 |
| Mitchill's | -0.92 | -7.36 | -1.65 |
| My provisional | +1.27 | -8.99 | +0.73 |

- A against hold, S1 to S7: 0 / +22.61 / 0 / +10.67 / +31.14 / 0 / 0. It is never worse in any column, and +9.13 expected at my weights.
- A's worst column is S6 at -16.29, the same as hold's, so A adds no downside.
- It spends nothing unless an airframer selects P&W this round.

5. Miss-a-cycle test [PX-0071]. I said this of RTX's businesses in general; applying it to GTF2 is inference.
- If NGSA flies without us (S3 -16.25, S6 -16.29), we lose our half of the A320neo slot. That is the largest exposure on the board.
- Only a selection repairs it, and 2030 is the only round in which a GTF2 can be ready for a 2030 airframe; a 2035 launch is ready in 2041.

The dividend first and foremost [PX-0081], then debt back to pre-ASR levels before buybacks [P-0686][P-0669]. Never fund an engine by cutting the dividend; Mitchill confirms.
Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]: no discount, concession or free upgrade in other moves or in the statement to win a selection.
Disclosure limits: no entry into service earlier than launch + 6, no durability claim that is not yet proven, and nothing about an airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062].
No widebody engine [PX-0027].

The Board's would-veto list, carried in: (1) an unconditional launch with an edge below +$0.5B; (2) a Joint Venture commitment this round; (3) any case that books an unrecorded selection, a later Airbus or Boeing code switch to P&W, or an unrecorded Rolls-Royce commitment; (4) any item with an unresolved Mitchill or Eddy veto, a red-line flag or an entry in overrides; (5) any item that can lose more than its own $2B against hold in a plausible column, or is not ready by the EIS it serves; (6) any spend that strains the dividend.
Premium cap: doctrine and objective premiums together stay at or under $1B. The Board passes an item that trails hold only as a declared premium of at most $0.5B that serves the objective.

Why launch_if_selected:

No unconditional launch on present numbers. Its edge over launch_if_selected is about -0.5 to -0.6 at plausible weights. The option it keeps open, a later code switch to P&W, cannot be booked. Joint Venture held. Rolls-Royce is not on the record, and no airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. The GTF is the architecture of the future [PX-0014], so GTF2 comes first. Revisit in 2035 if Rolls-Royce commits publicly or an airframe names code 1, 4, 5 or 7.

A trigger on a shared code (6 or 7) is declared as doctrine relief.

My provisional weights, before Neil's: S1 0.25, S2 0.20, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.15, S6 0.10, S7 0.10. Expected column S1; expected PV about +1.3.

Other moves (public): the GTF fleet durability kit, offered through MRO at value, not given away [PX-0088][PX-0100]; no pricing concession to any airframer.

Proposed disclosure (Neil to check the figures, Shane the readiness): 'The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: gtf2_solo: launch_if_selected; jv_with_rr: hold.

gtf2_solo launch_if_selected. 2030 is the only round in which GTF2 can be ready (2036) for an airframe launched now (EIS 2037 or 2040). A 2035 launch is ready in 2041, too late for every 2030 airframe. The order fires only if a live airframe selects a P&W code (2, 6, 7) this round and GTF2 is ready by its EIS, so the board's trigger itself enforces my readiness rule. It ties the launch to a customer and keeps engineering on the fleet until then. Grid row 'GTF2 Solo if selected' reads 0.00 / +6.36 / -16.25 / +10.29 / +14.85 / -16.29 / 0.00, against 'GTF2: hold' at 0.00 / -16.25 / -16.25 / -0.38 / -16.29 / -16.29 / 0.00. That is +22.61 (S2), +10.67 (S4) and +31.14 (S5), and zero elsewhere. Every trigger column uses a shared code (S2 code 6, S4 code 7, S5 codes 7 and 6). Calio declares that as doctrine relief. Technically, a shared code also leaves the airframer a second engine if ours ran late (inference).

Not an unconditional launch. My lever rule proposes it only into a P&W code already on the record, and nothing is on the record. It passes both my technical grounds (ready 2036; no live fleet problem), so this is not a veto. It is Mitchill's gate and the Board's +$0.5B bar. Advice only: in S1 and S7 it puts five years of engineers on an engine nobody asked for, then writes off $1.67B in 2035. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080].

jv_with_rr hold. Rolls-Royce's commitment is not on the record, and no live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. I have no evidence of my own on a Joint Venture, so this is seat doctrine plus P-1233. The call is Calio's.

ANSWERS TO CALIO'S ASKS
1. Proposal: as above.

2. Readiness and durability.
- Ready 2036 against NGSA 2037 (1 year of margin), the 7-year fps 2037 (1 year) and the 10-year or Embraer fps 2040 (4 years). The binding test passes.
- I cannot prove durability in 2030. The proof is test data that arrives in 2034-36.
- Advantage-level testing (3x the base programme [PX-0084]) at severe-environment conditions [PX-0128][PX-0122] fits six years only on three conditions: GTF2 stays a derivative inside the geared architecture (the mature gear is the enabler; a clean sheet is about 10 years [P-1269]), testing starts at launch, and nothing trades endurance testing for schedule.
- Our record: Advantage certification was aimed for mid-2024 and came in 2025, about a year late [PX-0128][P-0785]. Service entry was aimed for 2024 [PX-0017], with first Airbus deliveries around 2026, about two years late [P-1817]. The profile prior is +1.5-2 years.
- One year of margin covers the certification slip, not the service-entry slip. That is thin for 2037 and comfortable for 2040.
- So the public line is 'ready six years after launch; it enters service when its durability is proven'. We never promise a 2037 EIS. If test data put readiness past a selecting airframe's EIS, the EIS moves; the testing does not.

3. Joint Venture readiness.
- Formed in 2030 (Rolls-Royce must commit this round): ready 2036, so it could meet 2037 and 2040.
- Formed in 2035: ready 2041. That misses every 2030 airframe (2037, 2040) but meets 2035 airframes (NGSA or 7-year fps 2042, 10-year fps 2045).
- With a live 2030 GTF2 folded in: ready 2036, so it meets 2037 and 2040.
- Gear and core: P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and core as its own modules, sold into the Joint Venture under its own type data, with no licence or transfer [P-1233]. The Joint Venture shares risk and investment. Partners take shares and P&W stays in charge (profile §4). This is inference; my record has no Joint Venture.

4. Parts and capacity.
- The brief shows no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem. We deliver 816 NB engines a year in 2026-36 (85 A320s a month x 12 x 2 x 40%), our full A320neo share.
- The share fall from 26.7% to 24.4% is Boeing's deliveries rising from 510 to 654. It is not our supply.
- The board does not model AOG, powder metal or MRO slots.
- My last own-words count is June 2023: 10% of the fleet AOG, about 30 pacing parts, castings +40% [PX-0120][PX-0123][PX-0125]. The company file projects about 350 AOG on average through 2026 [PX-0300]. I have no 2030 count and won't reassure beyond the data.
- GTF2 development takes engineers, test cells and test-engine parts, not production pacing parts. The pressure comes with the production ramp from 2036. In S2 and S5 the NGSA replaces the A320neo lines, so our OE volume transfers rather than stacks (inference from rules.md).
- Powder metal came from a capacity ramp [P-1040], so any GTF2 capacity is qualified before it runs at rate. Fleet spares keep priority over GTF2 test hardware [PX-0123][PX-0080].

5. Engineering load.
- Option A: nothing unless we are selected, then one programme. S5 is the heaviest case: one engine, two installations, peaking 2035-37.
- Option B: none.
- Options C and F: one programme from 2030 for certain. In S1 and S7 that is five years on an unselected engine.
- Options D and E: in S7, a Joint Venture forms in 2030 with no airframe to serve.
- The Advantage engineering is shifting to other priorities [PX-0351] and the fleet kit runs from 2026 [PX-0088]. One development at a time is affordable; I would not advise two. The board has no strain charge, so this is my judgement.

6. Technical veto check, both grounds.
- A: passes both.
- B: no launch, so nothing to test.
- C: passes both. I don't propose it; engineering-load advice only.
- D, E and F: pass my two grounds (no airframe's EIS at risk, no draw on parts), but fail my Joint Venture conditions (no trigger, no gear-and-core terms). That is not a veto ground; I propose hold.

No binding veto on any option.

DISCLOSURE CHECK on Calio's draft: 'ready six years later, in 2036, and it will not enter service until its durability is proven' passes. There is no EIS before launch + 6 and no claim of proven durability. Optional wording: 'it will not enter service until every life-limited part has full life', stated as a condition, not as a claim.

tests.name: Readiness and durability by EIS (veto ground 1)
tests.threshold: Binding: GTF2 ready year (launch + 6) no later than the selecting airframe's EIS. The Joint Venture engine is ready 6 years after formation, or at the ready year of a folded-in solo if earlier (rules.md).
tests.numbers: GTF2 launch 2030, ready 2036. Live 2030 airframes: NGSA EIS 2037 (S2, S5), 7-year fps EIS 2037, 10-year fps EIS 2040 (S4 per the brief; S5 fps 2037 or 2040), Embraer fps EIS 2040. 2036 <= 2037 and 2036 <= 2040. launch_if_selected fires only if GTF2 is ready by the selecting airframe's EIS (rules.md), so it cannot trigger into an airframe it cannot serve. A 2035 GTF2 is ready in 2041 and misses every 2030 airframe.

tests.name: Durability margin for severe-environment testing (advice only, not a veto ground)
tests.threshold: About 1 year between ready year and EIS (inference from my own certification slip and the profile's +1.5-2 year derivative slip prior)
tests.numbers: Margin 1 year on NGSA and 7-year fps (2037 - 2036); 4 years on 10-year and Embraer fps (2040 - 2036). Record: Advantage certification aimed mid-2024, came 2025 (about +1 year); service entry aimed 2024, first Airbus deliveries about 2026 (about +2 years); profile prior +1.5-2 years. One year covers the certification slip, not the service-entry slip: at the minimum for 2037, ample for 2040. Requires Advantage-level testing (3x base) from launch, GTF2 kept a derivative of the geared architecture, and no compression to hold a date.

tests.name: Full life at entry into service, and disclosure
tests.threshold: All life-limited parts at full life at EIS; no public GTF2 EIS earlier than launch + 6 (2036); no durability claim not yet proven
tests.numbers: Calio's draft says 'ready six years later, in 2036, and it will not enter service until its durability is proven': no EIS before 2036, no claim of proven durability. Full-life LLPs are a condition for EIS, not a claim.

tests.name: Pacing parts and capacity (veto ground 2)
tests.threshold: If the brief or bulletin shows a live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, the fleet comes first and an unconditional launch fails; if none is shown, pass and note that the board does not model parts
tests.numbers: No live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem in the 2030 brief or bulletin. P&W delivers 816 NB engines a year in 2026-36 (85 A320s a month x 12 x 2 x 40%), its full A320neo share. The share fall from 26.7% to 24.4% (2026-29) comes from Boeing NB deliveries rising 510 to 654, not from P&W supply. The board does not model AOG, powder metal or MRO slots. My last own-words count is June 2023: 10% of the fleet AOG, about 30 pacing parts, castings +40%. No 2030 count is in evidence. launch_if_selected is conditional, so the ground-2 bar on an unconditional launch is not engaged.

tests.name: Contain first

tests.numbers: No quality escape in the 2030 brief or bulletin.

tests.name: Engineering load (advice only; no strain charge on this board)

tests.numbers: A: no programme unless selected, then one (S5: one engine, two installations, heaviest in 2035-37). B: none. C and F: one programme for certain from 2030; in S1 and S7 five years of engineering go into an unselected engine, written off at 2 x 5/6 = $1.67B in 2035. D and E: in S7 a Joint Venture forms in 2030 with no airframe to serve. The Advantage engineering is shifting to other priorities and the fleet kit runs from 2026.

tests.name: Single aisle

tests.numbers: No widebody move is proposed; this board has none for P&W.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
1. A later bulletin shows a live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem (an AOG wave or a powder-metal-type escape). Then the fleet comes first: contain it with a dated recovery before any new commitment, no unconditional launch (ground 2), and launch_if_selected only if the trigger does not pull pacing parts before the fleet's recovery date.
2. Severe-environment test data or a GTF2 plan that puts readiness after a selecting airframe's EIS. Then I veto entry into service on that airframe (ground 1) and do not compress testing.
3. An airframer puts a code that includes P&W on the public record. Then I propose a launch into it in its year, with the durability programme intact.
4. Rolls-Royce commits publicly, or a live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Then I set out the Joint Venture technical conditions (ready by EIS; P&W keeps the gear and core as its own modules) and leave the commit to Calio.
5. Mitchill's weights show the unconditional launch clearing zero and the Board's +$0.5B with 2035 named as the cancel round. That would be his and the Board's call, not my proposal; I have no technical objection.
ops.memo:
Bad number first. The biggest number on this grid is minus 16.29: NGSA in service without us. No engine order fixes that; only a selection does. Our narrowbody share slid from 26.7% to 24.4%, but that's Boeing's MAX ramp, not our shops: we still ship 816 engines a year, our full 40% of the A320neo.

My proposal: GTF2 launch_if_selected, Joint Venture on hold. Launched in 2030, GTF2 is ready in 2036. An NGSA or 7-year fps launched now enters service in 2037; a 10-year or Embraer fps in 2040. One year of margin on NGSA, four on the fps. A year is the least I want for severe-environment testing, and the Advantage certified about a year late. So Advantage-level testing from day one, every life-limited part at full life at entry into service, and no compressing it to hold a date. If the data aren't in, it doesn't fly.

Parts: the brief shows no live fleet, quality or supply problem; the board doesn't model parts. My last count is June 2023: 10% of the fleet down, about 30 pacing parts. I have no 2030 AOG count, and I won't tell you there's no surprise coming. A conditional launch takes nothing from the fleet unless we're selected.

No unconditional launch from me: no P&W code is on the record. The Joint Venture waits for Rolls-Royce, and any deal keeps our gear and core.

My record is one event, June 2023; where it's silent, I've used the seat's doctrine.

other_moves.move: GTF fleet durability kit (Hot Section kit) offered through MRO at value
other_moves.detail: We keep offering the GTF durability upgrade to operators through our MRO network at value. It is sold, not given away, and it is not tied to any airframe campaign [PX-0088][PX-0100]. It has no effect on the game board. It keeps the fleet ahead of a new engine [PX-0080].

other_moves.move: Standard commercial terms on GTF2; no launch-style discounts
other_moves.detail: Any GTF2 offer to Airbus or Boeing is on standard terms. There is no launch discount, concession or free upgrade to win a selection [PX-0055]. Mitchill's ground 3 (terms) passes. A rival's price does not move the answer.

other_moves.move: GTF2 durability programme staged for a triggered launch
other_moves.detail: If launch_if_selected fires, testing starts at launch at Advantage level (3x the base programme) under severe-environment conditions [PX-0084][PX-0128]. GTF2 stays a derivative of the geared architecture. Every life-limited part is at full life at entry into service, and no endurance testing is traded for schedule. If test data put readiness past a selecting airframe's EIS, the EIS moves and the testing does not. Fleet spares keep priority over GTF2 test hardware (Eddy). The 2035 cancel test for a live 2030 GTF2 follows Mitchill's rule: cancel only if the 2035 brief's cancel row beats its hold row, judged on the remaining $0.33B.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce: no commitment; revisit in 2035
other_moves.detail: We revisit only if Rolls-Royce commits on the public record or a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7). If we commit, P&W keeps the gear and the core as its own modules, with no licence or transfer [P-1233].

decision.public_statement: Bad news first. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Our share of narrowbody engine deliveries has slipped from 26.7% in 2026 to 24.4% in 2029 as the market mix moved, though we still deliver our full share of the A320neo. We control what we can control. Pratt & Whitney will launch its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it, as sole or shared source, provided GTF2 can be ready by that airframe's entry into service. GTF2 is ready six years from launch, so a launch this year is ready in 2036. It will not enter service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. It builds on the durability work we are doing on the GTF fleet today. The offer is on standard terms, with no launch discounts; these are responsible bets with responsible paybacks. We are not committing to a Joint Venture today. We will consider one only once a partner's commitment, or an airframer's demand for one, is on the record, and any partnership will share risk and investment, never our core technology. The airframers will speak for their own programmes. The dividend comes first, and this plan needs no change to it or to our path on debt.
decision.rationale:
EXCO DELIBERATION, ROUND 1 (2030). Decided by the team rule.

1. Starting point: Eddy's proposal, gtf2_solo launch_if_selected and jv_with_rr hold. Mitchill recommends the same orders, so both memos and the Board's guidance converge on Option A.

2. Binding vetoes struck:
- Mitchill, ground 2 (carrying an unselected engine), binding: the unconditional launch (C and F). Its edge over launch_if_selected is -0.73 at his weights, -0.64 at the Board's and -0.64 at my final weights. It is still about -0.5 with the 2035 cancel written in at a $1.67B write-off. Break-even needs p(S6) at 0.585 of the S1+S6+S7 mass; I have 0.10 of 0.50 = 0.20. It also fails the Board's +$0.5B bar. No objective premium buys a hedge that fails ground 2.
- Mitchill, ground 4 (booking unproven upside), binding: the Joint Venture commitment (D, E and F). Rolls-Royce has no commitment on the record and no live code includes Rolls-Royce. Committing is -2.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere, a weighted -0.20.
- Eddy: no binding veto on any option. His readiness check passes.
- Board: it vetoes the same two items, and approves launch_if_selected or hold.
- I accept every veto and revise nothing, because A carries no veto. 'overrides' is empty.

3. The safety and durability constraint, set first [PX-0035][PX-0073]:
- A 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036. EIS is 2037 for NGSA and the 7-year fps (one year of margin) and 2040 for the 10-year and Embraer fps (four years).
- launch_if_selected cannot fire into an airframe GTF2 cannot serve.
- My own operating dates have slipped, by about two years on the Advantage [PX-0017][PX-0087], so I discount them. That is why the public line promises 'ready six years from launch' and not a 2037 entry into service.
- The binding condition, as Eddy wrote it: durability proven, every life-limited part at full life, no compressed testing. If the data are not in, the EIS moves.

4. Optimising inside the constraint. Option A has the best expected PV of A to F at every weight set tested:

| Weights | A | Hold (B) | C (unconditional launch) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Mine (final) | +0.96 | -8.17 | +0.31 |
| Mitchill's | -0.92 | -7.36 | -1.65 |
| My provisional | +1.27 | -8.99 | +0.73 |

- A against hold, S1 to S7: 0 / +22.61 / 0 / +10.67 / +31.14 / 0 / 0. It is never worse in any column, and +9.13 expected at my weights.
- A's worst column is S6 at -16.29, the same as hold's, so A adds no downside.
- It spends nothing unless an airframer selects P&W this round.

5. Miss-a-cycle test [PX-0071]. I said this of RTX's businesses in general; applying it to GTF2 is inference.
- If NGSA flies without us (S3 -16.25, S6 -16.29), we lose our half of the A320neo slot. That is the largest exposure on the board.
- Only a selection repairs it, and 2030 is the only round in which a GTF2 can be ready for a 2030 airframe; a 2035 launch is ready in 2041.
- A lets us answer a selection this round, so the test is met.
- My incrementalism bias ('mid-next decade' [PX-0093]) would risk missing a round-1 selection. launch_if_selected means I do not have to be right about the timing.

6. Visible demand [PX-0109][PX-0009]. Capital is committed only when a live airframe puts a P&W code on the record. The Board guidance applies that as the doctrine's committed-airframe test [P-0746][P-0737].

7. Tie-breaks:
- The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: A takes no engineers or parts from the fleet unless we are selected.
- 'Miss a cycle' beats 'cross that bridge' only on visible demand: A is exactly that rule.
- A rival's discount never moves the answer: none is in play, and we offer standard terms.

8. Doctrine relief, declared:
- Every trigger column uses a shared code: S2 code 6, S4 code 7, S5 codes 7 and 6. Sole source is doctrine [P-0746].
- I accept shared source as doctrine relief at $0. Insisting on sole source would forgo the whole +9.13.
- On NGSA a shared code is also franchise defence. We hold about 40% of the shared A320neo [PX-0058], and 40-50% of a shared platform is acceptable [P-1292]. This is doctrine, not my own record.

9. Premium and objective:
- Doctrine and the assigned objective point to the same order, so premium_b is 0 of the $1B cap.
- Restore credibility (a new P&W engine in service on a new airframe by 2050) is met if A triggers in S2, S4 or S5: GTF2 ready 2036, EIS 2037 or 2040. That is p = 0.40 at my weights.
- Capitalise on the GTF (ΔPV ≥ 0) holds in S1, S2, S4, S5 and S7, and fails in S3 and S6, where no order on this board can help.

10. Joint Venture held:
- I have no record of my own here (Low), so this is doctrine plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test.
- The trigger fails. The GTF is the architecture of the future [PX-0014], so GTF2 comes first. My architecture-loyalty bias is noted.
- Revisit in 2035 if Rolls-Royce commits publicly or an airframe names code 1, 4, 5 or 7. A 2035 Joint Venture is ready in 2041, or in 2036 if a live 2030 GTF2 folds in.

11. Dividend: the dividend comes first [PX-0081], then debt to pre-ASR levels [P-0686][P-0669]. If triggered, GTF2 costs $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the roughly $6B envelope (Mitchill), so no stretch is needed.

12. Watch items for 2035:
- Mitchill's cancel test for any live 2030 GTF2, judged on the remaining $0.33B, not the sunk $1.67B.
- Eddy's durability data against a 2037 EIS.
- Any public Rolls-Royce commitment.

Disclosure: I took Mitchill's advice wording ('provided GTF2 can be ready by that airframe's entry into service') and Eddy's full-life condition. The statement gives no EIS before launch + 6, claims no proven durability, and says nothing about an airframer's dates [PX-0062].

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighted heavily. I trust Neil's cash numbers over my own dates, and his gate binds me.
- His two binding vetoes (ground 2 on the unconditional launch, ground 4 on the Joint Venture) are on allowed grounds, and the grid supports them, so I accept both.
- His weights are more pessimistic than mine (S1 0.35, S3 0.15). At them A is -0.92 expected, but it still beats hold by +6.44 and is the best row, so the decision is robust to his view.
- I moved my weights toward his: S1 up 0.05 from my provisional 0.25, because nothing is on the record.
- I adopted his advice wording for the statement and his 2035 cancel test, judged on the remaining $0.33B rather than the sunk $1.67B.
- His envelope check ($0.33B a year, 5.6% of about $6B) and his dividend and debt confirmation answer my dividend test.
- His booked number is +0.00 (S1), so no upside is booked.
memo_weighing.ops:
His proposal is the starting point under the team rule, and I took it unchanged. His record rests on one event, June 2023, so my confidence in him is Low. Where his record is silent he applied seat doctrine and said so, and I weigh it on that basis.
- His readiness check binds me and passes: ready 2036 against EIS 2037 and 2040.
- I took his caution seriously: one year of margin on a 2037 EIS covers a certification slip but not a service-entry slip. Given my own dates have slipped [PX-0017][PX-0087], the statement promises no EIS. Durability proven and full-life LLPs are conditions of entry into service, and the EIS moves before the testing does.
- His parts report has no 2030 AOG count. He would not reassure beyond the data, and I respect that. Because launch_if_selected spends and draws nothing unless selected, it keeps the fleet first [PX-0080].
- I accept his engineering-load advice, one development at a time, as a further reason against the unconditional launch and the Joint Venture, though it is not a veto ground.
- His gear-and-core terms for any Joint Venture are carried into the 2035 revisit.
